cases.title: The Fire at Ferréol
cases.subtitle: A case for the Bureau of Occult Affairs
cases.intro:
Thursday 18 November 1993, fourth floor of head office, Lyon.

The letter came with the morning post, between two flying saucers over the Vercors and a subscriber who sees the Virgin Mary in a damp stain. Karim set it aside. Brown envelope, Saint-Étienne postmark, Monday the 15th. Block capitals in ballpoint, pressed so hard the pen nearly went through the paper.

{{d:lettre_fantome|“TO THE NEWSPAPER. FOR A MONTH NOW THE FIRE HAS BEEN BACK IN THE FERRÉOL FORGE. YOU CAN SEE IT AT NIGHT FROM RUE DE LA MONTAT, RED, LIKE IN THE DAYS OF THE CASTINGS. IT IS THE FOUNDRYMAN FROM 1911. THEY LEFT HIM IN THE IRON AND CAST THE PIECE ANYWAY. HE COMES BACK EVERY TIME SOMEONE TOUCHES THE WORKS. FERRÉOL WILL NOT BE A CAR PARK. THERE WILL BE MORE DEATHS. AN OLD FERRÉOL HAND.”}}

At ten o'clock, Odile comes down with that day's Stéphanois, folded open at the local news. {{p:faure|Bernard Faure}}, 52, project officer in the planning department at the {{l:mairie|town hall}}, found dead on Wednesday morning at the foot of a staircase in the old {{l:site_ferreol|Ferréol Works}}. The {{l:commissariat|police}} have concluded it was an accidental fall. Fourteen lines, no photo.

Jean-Loup Sarrazin has read both over Odile's shoulder. “A ghost announces a death, and the death arrives. That's a page. Are we agreed?”

Paul folds the letter in four and slips it into his raincoat pocket. “Granted.”

That same evening, you set up in an empty office at the {{l:redaction|Stéphanois newsroom}}, on rue de la République. The radiator makes more noise than heat.

introNotes.text: Found dead on the morning of Wednesday 17 November, at the foot of a staircase at Ferréol. The police concluded it was an accidental fall.
introNotes.label: Official version

introNotes.text: Posted in Saint-Étienne on Monday 15 November, the day before Faure died. Signed “an old Ferréol hand”.
According to the letter, a “fire” has been glowing there at night for a month, and a foundryman died there in 1911.
introNotes.label: The legend

cases.briefing: Carry out interviews and investigations. Each lead you read for the first time costs one hour before the deadline, and you only have 20; rereading is free. A place only appears on the map once someone has told you about it. Some addresses have to be looked up on the Minitel. Some people will only talk if you come back with the right piece of evidence. When you are ready, write your article: everything depends on it.

clues.title: The Stéphanois archives
clues.text:
The Stéphanois documentation department fits into a windowless room between the boiler room and the photo archive. The “Ferréol” folder holds eleven cuttings.

April: a full page, {{p:roussillon|Marcel Roussillon}}, deputy mayor for planning, in front of the forge in a hard hat. The project is backed by {{l:cabinet_vallenot|Groupe Vallenot}}, run by {{p:vallenot|Hervé Vallenot}}. July: three lines on page 9, the budget “revised to allow for decontamination”. September: the firm {{l:siege_ferrand|Ferrand Frères}}, run by {{p:ferrand|Roger Ferrand}}, also wins the contract for the {{l:parking_relais|Bellevue park-and-ride}}.

A short item from May quotes an opponent, {{p:chaptal|Marcel Chaptal}}, former CGT union rep at the forge: “You don't turn a graveyard into a business park.” The reporter adds that he can be found every day at the {{l:cheval_noir|Cheval Noir}}.

facts.text: Conversion into a business incubator, announced in April 1993. Budget “revised” in July for decontamination.
facts.label: The project

facts.text: Backs the Ferréol project together with Groupe Vallenot.
Ferrand Frères: main contractor at Ferréol, and at the Bellevue park-and-ride since September.
Former CGT union rep at the forge, opposed to the project: “You don't turn a graveyard into a business park.”

clues.title: Daniel Roche, crime editor
clues.text:
{{p:roche|Daniel Roche}} doesn't get up from his chair. He has kept his raincoat on, as if he has been about to leave any minute since 1971. “So you're the Lyon lot. The ghost people.” He taps a packet of Gitanes on the desk without taking one out.

Paul: “Faure called you last week.”

“Me? I get ten calls a day from cranks. Thirty years in the trade, I can spot them by the first sentence.” He turns back to his typewriter. “Faure was an accident. Young {{p:lacour|Lacour}} certified it, the superintendent signed off. Go and photograph your spooks.”

facts.text: Says he doesn't remember a call from Faure.
The doctor who certified Faure's death, according to Roche.

clues.speaker: roche

clues.title: The switchboard operator's log
clues.text:
The switchboard operator, Madame Peyrache, keeps everything in school exercise books, one per month. She lets you leaf through November while keeping an eye on her board, where three lights are blinking at once.

Saturday the 13th, in a slanting hand: “4:40 p.m. M. Faure, planning dept, asks for the crime desk. Put through to M. Roche.” In the margin, in pencil, the length of the call, which she always notes for internal billing: “4 min”.

“Monsieur Roche? Yes, he took it. He even shut his door.”

facts.text: Called the Stéphanois on Saturday 13 November at 4:40 p.m. Put through to Daniel Roche.
facts.label: On the phone

facts.text: Spoke to Faure for 4 minutes, with his door shut.

clues.button: Go back to Roche with the log
clues.title: Roche, second interview
clues.text:
You lay the photocopy of the log on {{p:roche|Roche}}'s typewriter. He looks at it for a while. “Four minutes. All right.” At last he lights a Gitane.

“He didn't want an article, your Faure. He asked me: ‘How much is a file like this worth to you?’ How much. Thirty years in the trade, nobody had ever tried that on me. I hung up.”

Paul: “And you never told anyone.”

“Who would I tell? {{l:cabinet_vallenot|Groupe Vallenot}} buys a full page from us every Thursday. You want me to write that a civil servant is selling papers about Ferréol?”

facts.text: Asked Roche: “How much is a file like this worth to you?”
facts.label: On the phone

facts.text: Groupe Vallenot buys a full-page advertisement in the Stéphanois every Thursday.

clues.speaker: roche

clues.button: Call Odile at the group's archives
clues.title: Odile and the foundryman of 1911
clues.text:
Odile picks up on the second ring, in Lyon. “Ferréol. I'll fax you what I have.” Twenty-two minutes later, the newsroom fax machine starts to screech.

[[fax]]

Karim reads the still-warm page over your shoulder. “No, wait. Like sixty per cent of the sightings fall near an anniversary.”

facts.text: Étienne Vial, 19-year-old foundryman, fell into the molten iron on 3 February 1911. The casting was not stopped.
André Ferrand, 39, crushed to death under a concrete shuttering panel on 14 March 1987. Roger refused to speak to the reporter.
facts.label: His brother

clues.fax:
GROUPE SARRAZIN · ARCHIVES DEPARTMENT · LYON
TO: BUREAU OF OCCULT AFFAIRS, C/O LE STÉPHANOIS · 2 PAGES

LE STÉPHANOIS, 3 FEBRUARY 1911, PAGE 4, RIGHT-HAND COLUMN
Accident at the Ferréol forge. A nineteen-year-old foundryman, Étienne Vial, fell into the casting ladle yesterday. The casting was not stopped. The piece, a rolling-mill wheel, has been shipped to Le Creusot.

LE STÉPHANOIS, 14 MARCH 1987, PAGE 11, BOTTOM LEFT
Montreynaud: builder crushed under shuttering panel. André Ferrand, 39, co-manager of Ferrand Frères, died on the Tower 12 building site. His brother Roger declined to comment.

(Handwritten, at the bottom of the page:) Nothing else on Ferréol between 1947 and 1990. Not a line. Odd. O.

clues.title: Yves's prints
clues.text:
Yves got the darkroom technician talking. On the morning of the 17th, the duty photographer went to Ferréol for the news item. The paper published nothing, but the contact sheet stayed in a drawer.

Yves lays it under the lamp and hands you his loupe. Frame number seven: the east wall, at eight o'clock. On the white letters, the paint is still glistening. Two drips run down to the pavement, and an empty paint tin stands against the wall.

Paul takes the ghost's letter out of his raincoat pocket and lays it next to the sheet. Yves looks at one, then the other. “Ferréol will not be a car park.” He says it again, more slowly: “Not a car park.”

facts.text: At 8 a.m. on the 17th, the paint of the slogan was still wet. An empty tin against the wall.
facts.label: East wall

clues.title: Marcel Roussillon, deputy mayor for planning
clues.text:
{{p:roussillon|Marcel Roussillon}} receives you standing up, his door open onto the corridor. On his right ring finger, a gold signet ring engraved with a salamander in flames. He turns it as he talks.

“We all miss Bernard Faure very much in the department. A conscientious officer.” On the budget: “We followed the technical advice. You can't rush decontamination.”

You haven't asked anything about Tuesday evening yet. “And as for that evening, we were in the council meeting until half past ten. Anyone can tell you that.”

A chime sounds in the corridor. He is on his feet before you.

facts.text: Wears a gold signet ring engraved with a salamander in flames.
Says, without being asked, that he was in the council meeting until 10:30 p.m.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

clues.speaker: roussillon

clues.title: The redevelopment file
clues.text:
A clerk from the department, her eyes red, leaves you the {{d:dossier_ferreol|Ferréol file}} while she goes to fetch a coffee. “It was his file. Monsieur Faure's.”

The decontamination plan runs to twelve pages: 3,000 tonnes of soil laden with hydrocarbons and metals, to be taken to the {{l:decharge|licensed landfill at Croix-de-l'Orme}}. The budget goes from 4 to 8.2 million francs by a council resolution in July, signed by {{p:roussillon|M. Roussillon}}, without a call for tenders. A line for “studies and fees” of 1.3 million, payable to an {{d:sci_delombre|SCI Delombre}} whose name appears nowhere else.

In the margin of the tonnage page, someone has written in pencil, then rubbed it out. All that remains is the trace of a question mark.

facts.text: 3,000 tonnes of contaminated soil to be taken to the Croix-de-l'Orme landfill.
facts.label: Tonnage

facts.text: Raised from 4 to 8.2 million francs in July, without a call for tenders. Resolution signed by Roussillon.
facts.label: Budget

facts.text: 1.3 million francs of “studies and fees” on Ferréol. No other trace at the town hall.

clues.button: Read the minutes of the council meeting
clues.title: The council meeting of 16 November
clues.text:
The minutes of the council meeting of Tuesday 16 November are already typed, photocopied and stapled.

Meeting opened at 6:30 p.m. School canteen budget: {{p:roussillon|M. Roussillon}} speaks at 10:15 p.m., three paragraphs on the price of a meal. Meeting closed at 10:30 p.m.

In the margin of one copy, an opposition councillor has scribbled: “Roussillon ran off, didn't stay for drinks.”

facts.text: Speaks at the council meeting at 10:15 p.m. Meeting closed at 10:30 p.m. Left in a hurry, without staying for drinks.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

clues.button: Ask for the site's phone bill
clues.title: The itemised bill for the watchman's hut
clues.text:
In the accounts department, a clerk digs out the {{d:facture_tel|itemised bill}} for line 77 33 61 08, “watchman's hut, Ferréol site”, paid for by the town. October and November fit on two sheets of perforated computer paper.

About thirty calls, nearly all in the daytime, to the town hall or to Ferrand Frères. The clerk has already walked off. Karim runs his finger down the columns.

clues.title: Hervé Vallenot, the developer
clues.text:
{{p:vallenot|Hervé Vallenot}} receives you standing in front of a scale model of the project: trees made of green sponge, little figures going nowhere. The room smells of stale cigarillo. “Ferréol is a fine project. A fine operation for the town.”

On Faure, he lowers his voice half a tone. “A tragedy. I knew him from a distance, it was the council officers who handled the file.”

Paul: “So you were at Ferréol on Tuesday evening.”

“Tuesday? I was at home. Alone, my wife was at her mother's in Lyon. An evening in front of the television.” He smiles. “Nothing very exciting.”

You ask who poured the new concrete slab. “That's a technical matter. Ask Roger Ferrand.”

As he shows you out, he slips a {{d:carte_vallenot|business card}} into Paul's pocket. Groupe Vallenot, Hervé Vallenot, Chairman. Car phone: 07 42 18 63. “For your nice little article. Don't hesitate.”

facts.text: Says he spent the evening alone at home, his wife at her mother's in Lyon.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

facts.text: Says he only knew the Ferréol file “from a distance”.
Hervé Vallenot, Chairman. Car phone: 07 42 18 63.

clues.speaker: vallenot

clues.button: Take advantage of the secretary's absence
clues.title: Vallenot's office
clues.text:
The secretary goes downstairs to fetch the post and leaves the door ajar.

On a badly closed binder, an {{d:facture_delombre|invoice from SCI Delombre}}: “Urban strategy consultancy, Ferréol project, 1,300,000 F”. No report, no appendix, paid in cash, signed Maurice Delombre, managing partner.

On {{p:vallenot|Vallenot}}'s walnut desk, next to the car phone in its carrying case, a crystal ashtray and an open {{d:cigarillos|box of Dutch cigarillos}}. The cigarillos have white plastic tips.

Through the window, in the courtyard, a midnight-blue Renault Safrane is parked at an angle.

facts.text: 1.3 million francs for “urban strategy consultancy”, with no report or appendix. Signed Maurice Delombre, managing partner.
Dutch cigarillos with white plastic tips, on Vallenot's desk.
A midnight-blue Safrane, parked in the offices' courtyard.
facts.label: His car

clues.button: Meet Igier at the café opposite
clues.title: Lieutenant Igier
clues.text:
{{p:igier|Igier}} meets you at the bar of the café opposite, never at the station. “On the 17th at 6:40 a.m., the patrol proceeded to the scene, where it observed…” He breaks off and puts down his cup. “Look. We got there, he was dead, we called the doctor.”

He slides a photocopy of the {{d:constat|report}} across to you. “Victim found at the foot of the metal staircase.” No sketch, no photos. The death certificate is signed by {{p:lacour|Dr Pierre Lacour}}.

“I'm not the one who typed the report. Superintendent Borel did it himself, during the morning. Normally, when a civil servant dies on a building site, we handle it with kid gloves. Not this time.”

facts.text: “Victim found at the foot of the metal staircase.” No sketch or photos. Typed by Superintendent Borel himself.
Signed Faure's death certificate.

clues.speaker: igier

clues.button: Go back to Igier with the doctor's admission
clues.title: Igier, second interview
clues.text:
When you repeat what {{p:lacour|Lacour}} told you, {{p:igier|Igier}} stares into the bottom of his cup for a long time. “The time of death was established by…” He stops. “No. Listen.”

“On the 17th at 8:10 a.m., the superintendent got a phone call. I was in his office. He said ‘Yes, Monsieur le Maire-adjoint’ three times and hung up. Afterwards he told me not to bother about the position of the body.”

He puts a banknote on the counter. “It was {{p:roussillon|Roussillon}}. You didn't get that from me.”

facts.text: Superintendent Borel takes a call at 8:10 a.m. and answers “Yes, Monsieur le Maire-adjoint”. According to Igier, it was Roussillon.
facts.label: Wednesday 17th

facts.text: After that call, the superintendent told Igier “not to bother about the position of the body”.

clues.speaker: igier
clues.buttonAlone: Meet Igier with the doctor's admission
clues.titleAlone: Igier, faced with the doctor's admission

clues.title: Dr Lacour
clues.text:
{{p:lacour|Dr Lacour}}'s surgery smells of ether and damp carpet. He sees you between two patients, without asking you to sit down.

“Killed outright, I imagine. A four-metre fall onto steel, it's very typical. Nothing alarming.” He looks at his watch, then at the clock.

Paul: “So you got there around six.”

“Seven. They called me at a quarter to seven. Everything was very typical. These things happen, on building sites.”

facts.text: Called at 6:45 a.m., arrived at Ferréol at 7. Speaks of being “killed outright”.

clues.speaker: lacour

clues.button: Go back to Lacour with the watchman's account
clues.title: Lacour, second interview
clues.text:
You tell {{p:lacour|Lacour}} what the watchman saw: the body by the door, two metres from the staircase, eyes open. He closes the surgery door. For the first time, he doesn't look at his watch.

“The rigor, the lividity… He died between midnight and one in the morning. Not at ten.” He takes off his glasses. “He wasn't killed outright. It took him a long time. Two hours, perhaps. He must have been cold.”

Paul: “And you wrote ‘immediate death’.”

“The superintendent was there. He told me a family doesn't need to read that kind of detail. I'm sixty-one, monsieur.”

facts.text: Between midnight and one in the morning, according to Dr Lacour. Not killed outright.
facts.label: Time of death

facts.text: Wrote “immediate death” at the superintendent's request.

clues.speaker: lacour
clues.buttonAlone: See Dr Lacour with the watchman's account
clues.titleAlone: Dr Lacour, faced with the watchman's account

clues.title: Colette Faure, the widow
clues.text:
{{p:colette|Colette Faure}} shows you into a kitchen where everything is tidied away, except a pile of post she isn't opening. “Bernard always leaves at eight. Left.”

On Tuesday he said he had a meeting. He went out at seven in the evening with his {{d:dossier_bleu|blue folder}}, “the one he hadn't let out of his sight since the summer”. What was in it? “I don't know. Work papers.”

On the fridge, under a magnet shaped like the Virgin of Fourvière, a photo of a young woman in front of a lecture hall. “Our girl. Studying law in Lyon. He does overtime for her. Did.”

facts.text: Left home at 7 p.m., “for a meeting”, with his blue folder.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

facts.text: Bernard hadn't let it out of his sight since the summer. Colette says she doesn't know what was in it.
Their daughter is studying law in Lyon.

clues.speaker: colette

clues.title: Bernard Faure's study
clues.text:
Bernard's study is an old child's bedroom, balloon wallpaper under the shelves. The drawer where Colette expected to find the blue folder is empty.

In a folder marked “Bank”, the {{d:releves_faure|Crédit Agricole statements}}. The mortgage is three payments behind in June, then everything is paid up in August. Every month since, a cash deposit: 29,000 francs in August, 29,500 in September, 30,000 in October.

In the desk diary, on Tuesday the 16th, a single line: “10 p.m., F.”

facts.text: Mortgage three payments behind in June, paid up in August. Cash deposits: 29,000 F in August, 29,500 F in September, 30,000 F in October.
In his diary: “10 p.m., F.”
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

clues.button: Go back to Colette with the “B.F.” withdrawals
clues.title: Colette, second interview
clues.text:
You lay the photocopy of the “B.F.” withdrawals on the oilcloth. {{p:colette|Colette Faure}} reads it twice without a word. Then she gets up, opens her sewing box and takes a {{d:carnet_versements|small spiral notebook}} from under the reels of thread.

“Bernard writes everything down. Wrote. Even when he fills up the car.”

On one page, four lines in ballpoint. “R.F. 30” in August, in September, in October. In November: “R.F. 200?”, the question mark gone over several times.

“I found the envelopes in September. In a shoebox, on top of the wardrobe. I didn't ask. We had the mortgage, our girl in Lyon…”

She also puts a numbered {{d:ticket_consigne|orange ticket}} on the table. “It was in his wallet. I don't know what it's for.” It's a ticket from the left luggage office at {{l:consigne_gare|Châteaucreux station}}.

At the end of the table, Bernard's place is still laid.

facts.text: “R.F. 30” in August, September and October. “R.F. 200?” in November.
Found envelopes of banknotes in September, in a shoebox.
facts.label: What she was hiding

facts.text: Left luggage office at Châteaucreux station. Found in Bernard's wallet.

clues.speaker: colette
clues.buttonAlone: Visit Colette Faure with the “B.F.” withdrawals
clues.titleAlone: Colette Faure, faced with the “B.F.” withdrawals

clues.title: The Châteaucreux left luggage
clues.text:
The left luggage office at {{l:consigne_gare|Châteaucreux}} is a counter at the end of the concourse, under the clock. The attendant looks at the ticket, sighs, and comes back with a blue sports bag from a handball club.

Inside, a brown envelope: a {{d:copie_faure|copy of a file}}. Photocopies of the landfill's weighbridge tickets. Twelve flash photos of Ferrand Frères tipper lorries, at night, in the Ferréol yard. And a handwritten table: “Planned: 3,000 t. Removed: 400 t. Remaining: ?”

At the bottom of the bag, a spare pair of socks and an opened packet of biscuits. Karim looks at the socks for longer than at the documents.

facts.text: Photocopies of the landfill's weighbridge tickets. Twelve photos of Ferrand lorries at night at Ferréol. Table: “Planned: 3,000 t. Removed: 400 t. Remaining: ?”

clues.title: Ahmed Bensaïd, the watchman
clues.text:
{{p:bensaid|Ahmed Bensaïd}} opens the gate without a word more than necessary. Twenty years as a watchman.

“It may be that I heard voices, Monsieur le journaliste. Around ten o'clock. Over by the forge workshop. I didn't go down, it's not my job.”

The lorries? “It may be there were some, at night. For a month now. Ferrand's.”

Paul: “So you saw who was driving.”

“No, monsieur. I don't look at what's none of my business.” He walks you back out. “For the history of the works, see {{p:chaptal|Marcel Chaptal}} instead. He's at the {{l:cheval_noir|Cheval Noir}} every day.”

facts.text: Says he heard voices around 10 p.m., over by the forge workshop. “I didn't go down.”
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

facts.text: Ferrand's lorries have been coming at night for a month, according to the watchman.
facts.label: At night

clues.speaker: bensaid

clues.title: Surveying the site
clues.text:
The sign at the entrance announces a project on hold since September. Client: {{l:cabinet_vallenot|Groupe Vallenot}}, {{p:vallenot|H. Vallenot}}. Main contractor: {{l:siege_ferrand|Ferrand Frères}}, {{p:ferrand|R. Ferrand}}.

In the east wing, a new concrete slab covers the foot of the metal staircase, still dark with damp. All around, the ground is black with mill scale and churned earth. Against a pillar, two floodlights on tripods and a generator, the cables neatly coiled. Under a pallet, a delivery note: “Concrete, 8 m³, 17/11/93, received {{p:mounier|G. Mounier}}”.

At the back gate, twin-tyre tracks in the mud, and four scraps of paper plastered against the wire fence by the rain.

On the boundary wall, on the east side, in white letters a metre high: FERRÉOL WILL NOT BE A CAR PARK.

Yves takes three photos of the wall, two of the slab, one of the floodlights.

facts.text: New concrete slab at the foot of the staircase, on a site on hold since September.
facts.label: East wing

facts.text: Two site floodlights and a generator in the workshop.
facts.label: At night

facts.text: Slogan in white letters: “FERRÉOL WILL NOT BE A CAR PARK”.
facts.label: East wall

facts.text: Took delivery of 8 m³ of concrete at Ferréol on 17 November.

clues.button: Go back to Bensaïd with the dealer's register
clues.title: Bensaïd, second interview
clues.text:
{{p:bensaid|Ahmed Bensaïd}} looks at the photocopy of the {{d:livre_police|dealer's register}} for a long time. Then he shuts the door of the hut.

“It may be that…” He stops. “No. I was at the back gate, with {{p:berthet|Berthet}}. The cast iron goes for scrap anyway.”

After that he speaks without any “may be”, all in one go, his hands flat on the table. “At about twenty to eleven, on my way back, there was a car outside the entrance. A midnight-blue Safrane. Not a local car. In the morning, at half past six, I did my round. The gentleman wasn't at the foot of the staircase. He was near the door. His eyes were open. I closed them for him.”

He opens a drawer and puts a matchbox on the table. Inside, {{d:megots|four cigarillo butts}} with white plastic tips. “They were next to him. I don't know why I kept them.”

On the doorstep, he adds: “That night, someone went into my hut. The phone was hanging off the hook. And old {{p:chaptal|Chaptal}}, from the {{l:cheval_noir|Cheval Noir}}, was hanging around along the east wall at about nine. It was Doctor {{p:lacour|Lacour}} who came, in the morning.”

facts.text: Sells the site's scrap iron to Berthet. On the evening of the 16th, he was at the back gate.
facts.label: What he was hiding

facts.text: Found at 6:30 a.m. near the door, not at the foot of the staircase. Eyes open.
facts.label: Morning of the 17th

facts.text: Cigarillos with white plastic tips, found next to the body by the watchman.
A midnight-blue Safrane outside the entrance around 10:40 p.m. Someone went into the watchman's hut and used the phone.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

facts.text: Seen along the east wall around 9 p.m., according to the watchman.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

clues.speaker: bensaid
clues.buttonAlone: Show the dealer's register to the watchman
clues.titleAlone: Ahmed Bensaïd, faced with the dealer's register

clues.button: Examine the floor near the door
clues.title: Near the workshop door
clues.text:
The watchman shows you the spot, then goes back to his hut. He doesn't want to look.

The new slab stops two metres short of the workshop door. Beyond it, the brick floor is covered in a black dust of mill scale that nobody has swept. You can make out finger marks in it, parallel, running from the edge of the slab towards the door. They stop fifty centimetres short of the threshold.

In a groove between two bricks, Yves finds a broken fingernail. He photographs it without flash, then with, and leaves it where it is.

facts.text: Finger marks in the mill scale, from the edge of the slab towards the door. They stop 50 cm short of the threshold. A broken fingernail between two bricks.
facts.label: Near the door

clues.title: Marcel Chaptal
clues.text:
{{p:chaptal|Marcel Chaptal}} speaks low, his elbow on the zinc counter, in front of a glass of red he won't finish. “Ferréol, lad, I started there the year of the big miners' strike, in forty-eight. Thirty years at the forge.”

He tells the story of the 1911 foundryman as if he'd been there. “They left him in the molten iron. The piece went out all the same. It must still be turning somewhere, that piece.”

The fire at night? “Everyone's seen it, on rue de la Montat. Ask around.”

And him, on Tuesday evening? “Here. At the bar, all evening. Ask {{p:jeannot|Jeannot}}.”

facts.text: Says he spent the evening at the bar of the Cheval Noir. “Ask Jeannot.”
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

facts.text: According to Chaptal, the whole neighbourhood sees the forge's “fire” at night, from rue de la Montat.
facts.label: The legend

clues.title: Jeannot, landlord of the Cheval Noir
clues.text:
{{p:jeannot|Jeannot}} wipes the glasses one by one, holding them up to the light, taking his time.

“Marcel? Tuesday?” He puts down one glass and picks up another. “He had his first round at seven, his second at eight. The third one he had after ten. In between, no Marcel.”

He lowers his voice. “He came back with his hands covered in white paint. He said to me: ‘If anyone asks, I was here.’ Me, I answer what I'm asked. You're asking.”

facts.text: Away from the Cheval Noir from 8 p.m. until after 10, according to Jeannot. Came back with his hands covered in white paint.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

clues.speaker: jeannot

clues.button: Go back to Chaptal about the paint on the wall
clues.title: Chaptal, second interview
clues.text:
When you mention the paint, {{p:chaptal|Chaptal}} puts his glass down. “All right. Yes. The wall was me. And the letter. And two more, to Faure, unsigned. To scare him. To make him stop with his car park.”

He rubs his fingers. There is still white under his nails. “On Tuesday, around nine, Faure's car was in the cul-de-sac. A grey Peugeot 405. And at ten to ten, Ferrand's tipper lorry arrived. With the boss at the wheel, lad. {{p:ferrand|Ferrand}} himself, who never drives. I left. I didn't want to be seen with my paint tin.”

He looks out at the street. “The foundryman is just stories. I'm the one who tells them.”

facts.text: Painted the slogan on the east wall, wrote the letter to the Bureau and sent two anonymous letters to Faure.
facts.label: What he was hiding

facts.text: Arrived at Ferréol around 9:50 p.m., alone at the wheel of the tipper lorry, according to Chaptal.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

facts.text: His grey 405 was in Impasse des Fondeurs around 9 p.m., according to Chaptal.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

clues.title: Roger Ferrand
clues.text:
{{p:ferrand|Roger Ferrand}} doesn't sit down, and neither do you. In the shed, a radio blares RTL over the noise of a compressor nobody switches off.

“Tuesday evening? Why, where should I have been?”

Paul: “At Ferréol, with Faure.”

“And what would I have been doing at Ferréol, on a site that's on hold?” He wipes his hands on his overalls, slowly, one hand then the other. His wedding ring bites into a swollen finger. “I was at home. Ask {{p:simone|my wife}}, she's in the office at the back. You think she'll tell you any different?”

facts.text: Says he spent the evening of the 16th at home. “Ask my wife.”
facts.label: Alibi

clues.speaker: ferrand

clues.button: Take a look at the accounts
clues.title: The Ferrand Frères accounts
clues.text:
The glass-walled office at the back is empty: {{p:simone|Simone Ferrand}} has gone to the bank. On the table, the {{d:compta_ferrand|cash book}} lies open at November.

Three transfers of 430,000 francs to {{d:sci_delombre|SCI Delombre}}, in June, July and September. Further down, in the cash withdrawals column, in a bookkeeper's round hand:

12/08 · B.F. · 30,000
13/09 · B.F. · 30,000
12/10 · B.F. · 30,000
16/11 · B.F. · 50,000

In the {{d:agenda_ferrand|site diary}}, on Tuesday 16 November, in pencil, pressed hard: “Ferréol 10 p.m.”

In a corner, a wood-burning stove is roaring. In the ashtray beneath it, under the grey ash, a corner of blue card that didn't burn and a binder clip twisted by the heat.

The Post Office calendar hangs crooked. Behind it, you can make out the metal of a small safe door.

facts.text: 30,000 F on 12 August, 13 September and 12 October. 50,000 F on 16 November.
facts.label: “B.F.” withdrawals

facts.text: Tuesday 16 November: “Ferréol 10 p.m.”
In the ashes, a corner of blue card and a binder clip.
facts.label: The stove

facts.text: Three transfers of 430,000 F from Ferrand Frères, in June, July and September.

clues.button: Examine the safe behind the calendar
clues.title: Roger Ferrand's safe
clues.text: The Post Office calendar hangs from a nail. The pages from January to October have been torn off, except one, kept behind November: March, with the 14th circled in black felt pen. Behind it, a small safe door set into the breeze-block wall, with a four-digit dial.

clues.title: Simone Ferrand
clues.text:
{{p:simone|Simone Ferrand}} keeps the books in a glass-walled office at the back of the shed, between a metal filing cabinet and a plastic ficus. “Roger says you've no business here.”

Tuesday evening? “Roger came home at nine. As usual.” She answered before you'd finished the question. “Roger says it's a good season, we've got work till the spring.”

The night shift? “{{p:mounier|Gérard Mounier}} runs it. Roger says we're not to talk to the papers.”

facts.text: Claims Roger came home at 9 p.m. on the 16th. Answered before the question was finished.
Foreman of the Ferrand Frères night shift.

clues.speaker: simone

clues.button: Go back to Simone about the lorry
clues.title: Simone, second interview
clues.text:
You tell her Ferrand's lorry was at Ferréol on Tuesday evening. {{p:simone|Simone}} doesn't deny it. She puts away one pencil, then another.

“Roger says…” She stops. “He came home at twenty past eleven. I looked at the alarm clock. He went into the utility room. He washed his trousers himself, by hand, in the sink. He never does that. He doesn't even know where we keep the washing powder.”

She looks towards the shed, where her husband is talking loudly on the phone. “There was black dust in the water.”

facts.text: Came home at 11:20 p.m. on the 16th, according to Simone. Washed his own trousers during the night. Black dust in the water.
facts.label: Alibi

facts.text: Retracts her statement: Roger was not home at 9 p.m.

clues.buttonAlone: Ask Simone Ferrand about the lorry

clues.title: Gérard Mounier, foreman
clues.text:
{{p:mounier|Gérard Mounier}} talks to you on the ninth-floor landing, in a tracksuit, the door pulled shut behind him: his wife is asleep, she works nights at the hospital.

“I don't know anything. I do what I'm told.” The concrete on the 17th? “The boss said pour, so I poured.”

Paul: “And on the evening of the 16th, you were at Ferréol with your crew, then.”

“No. The boss said not to come on Tuesday. For once.” He hears what he has just said. “We'd been going every night for a month, and on Tuesday, no. That's all. The boss decides.”

facts.text: “The boss said not to come.” For the first time in a month.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

facts.text: Poured the new slab at Ferréol, on orders.
facts.label: Wednesday 17th

clues.speaker: mounier

clues.button: Go back to Mounier with the tonnages
clues.title: Mounier, second interview
clues.text:
You show him the figures: 3,000 tonnes planned, 400 delivered to the landfill. {{p:mounier|Mounier}} sits down on a step. “The boss said they'd pin this on me. I knew it.”

Since October, his crew has been digging at night in the east wing, tipping the black earth into the pits and pouring a slab on top. “It stinks of diesel, that earth. It burns your hands.”

He falls silent, then: “On the 17th, before we poured near the staircase, there were dark smears on the floor. I asked the boss. He said: ‘Pour.’”

facts.text: Since October, the night shift has been burying black earth that smells of diesel there, on Ferrand's orders.
facts.label: Under the slabs

facts.text: Before pouring near the staircase, saw dark smears on the floor. Ferrand: “Pour.”
facts.label: Wednesday 17th

clues.title: Lucien Berthet, scrap dealer
clues.text:
{{p:berthet|Lucien Berthet}}'s scrapyard fills the yard of an old glassworks on the bank of the Gier. Shells of Renault 4s, cast-iron radiators, a crane that creaks.

“Ferréol? Never set foot there, my friend.” He shows you round anyway. “Over there, copper, eighteen francs a kilo. There, aluminium. Cast iron's worth nothing, my friend. One franc twenty, on a good day.”

He kicks a pile of radiators. “Ferréol is cast iron. You can see it's no interest to me.”

facts.text: Says he has “never set foot” at Ferréol. “Cast iron's worth nothing.”

clues.speaker: berthet

clues.title: The scrapyard's dealer's register
clues.text:
Scrap dealers have to keep a {{d:livre_police|dealer's register}}, numbered and initialled by the gendarmerie. {{p:berthet|Berthet}}'s lies on the desk in the gatehouse, under a dirty cup. Berthet is out in the yard, at the crane.

The handwriting is slow, careful, full of spelling mistakes. “16/11/93 · 21:30 · Ferréol site back gait · seller A.B. · cast iron 1.2 t · 1,440 F cassh.”

The same line appears on 2 and 9 November. Always a Tuesday.

facts.text: “16/11/93, 21:30, Ferréol site, back gate, seller A.B., cast iron 1.2 t.” Same line on Tuesday 2 and Tuesday 9 November.
At the back gate of Ferréol at 9:30 p.m., according to his own register.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

clues.button: Go back to Berthet with his register
clues.title: Berthet, second interview
clues.text:
{{p:berthet|Berthet}} sees the open register in your hands and cuts the crane. “All right. I was there, my friend. Every Tuesday. It's not theft, it's salvage.”

Tuesday the 16th: arrived at half past nine, left at half past ten. “At about ten past ten, there was a scream inside the works. Just one. After that, nothing. The watchman said it was the cats.”

He spits on the ground. “In the yard, there was Ferrand's tipper lorry. Engine still warm. I put my hand on the bonnet as I went by. Habit.”

facts.text: A scream around 10:10 p.m., then nothing, according to Berthet. Ferrand's tipper lorry in the yard, engine still warm.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

facts.text: At the back gate from 9:30 to 10:30 p.m.
facts.label: Tuesday 16th

clues.button: Look at the register of deliveries
clues.title: The landfill register
clues.text:
The {{l:decharge|Croix-de-l'Orme landfill}} records its deliveries on {{d:registre_decharge|weighbridge slips}} stapled together by site. The attendant, who doesn't get many visitors, digs out the folder marked “Ferrand Frères, Ferréol”.

Twenty-two slips, all from July and August. At the bottom of the last one, the total, underlined twice: 400 tonnes.

“Nothing from them since September. They've finished, I suppose.” He leafs through again. “Odd, for a big job like that.”

facts.text: Ferrand Frères, Ferréol site: 22 weighings in July and August, 400 tonnes in all. Nothing since September.

clues.title: The park-and-ride building site
clues.text:
The Bellevue park-and-ride site, at least, is moving along. Three cranes, rows of shuttering panels, a sign: client {{l:cabinet_vallenot|Groupe Vallenot}}, main contractor {{l:siege_ferrand|Ferrand Frères}}.

The site manager, a jovial man, shows you the financing plan pinned up in his Portakabin. A line for “studies” of 900,000 francs, paid to {{d:sci_delombre|SCI Delombre}}. “Never seen anyone from their lot. Still, we've got the plans.” He shrugs and offers you an instant coffee.

facts.text: Also receives 900,000 F for “studies” on the park-and-ride site.

endings.title: The front page
endings.headline: Ferréol: the ghost had a car phone
endings.text:
On Saturday 27 November, the Occult Affairs page is not on page 14. It is on the front page, under a headline by Jean-Loup, who doesn't like being told no: “Ferréol: the ghost had a car phone”.

Roger Ferrand is charged with manslaughter. He says almost nothing, except one sentence to the examining magistrate, reported by Igier: “I pushed him. After that, it was the other one who decided.” Hervé Vallenot is charged with failing to assist a person in danger. His lawyers speak of a “tragic misunderstanding”. Groupe Vallenot cancels its Thursday advertising page.

The article hides nothing about Bernard Faure. Colette calls the newsroom on Monday. She doesn't shout. She only asks whether it was necessary. Paul says yes. He hangs up, and sits for a long time without relighting his cigarette.

endings.title: The martyr
endings.headline: Killed for trying to speak out
endings.text:
On Saturday 27 November, the article turns Bernard Faure into a whistleblower, killed for trying to expose a scandal. Ferrand and Vallenot are charged. The town holds a minute's silence outside the town hall.

Three weeks later, Ferrand's lawyer produces Faure's bank statements and the “B.F.” withdrawals before the magistrate. A rival daily runs the headline “The martyr who was getting paid”. The Stéphanois prints a correction on page 2. Jean-Loup says nothing, which is worse.

Colette Faure no longer answers the phone. On Bernard's grave, someone has left an empty envelope.

endings.title: The developer
endings.headline: Ferréol: building contractor charged
endings.text:
On Saturday 27 November, the article stands up: Roger Ferrand pushed Bernard Faure, and he is charged with manslaughter. He says nothing. He will say nothing until the trial.

Nobody mentions the Safrane, or the four cigarillo butts. Hervé Vallenot declares himself “deeply shocked” and “standing by the family”. The following Thursday, his advertising page appears in the Stéphanois as usual, with a photo of the Ferréol scale model: trees made of green sponge, little figures going nowhere.

At Ferréol, someone has swept away the mill scale by the workshop door. The finger marks are gone. Nobody knows who.

endings.title: The denial
endings.headline: The Ferréol ghost has not had its last word
endings.text:
The article comes out on Saturday 27 November. On Monday, the town hall issues a statement: the police investigation concluded it was an accident, and “certain journalists would do better to stick to ghosts”. Groupe Vallenot threatens to pull its advertising from every paper in the group.

Jean-Loup summons Paul. The door stays shut for an hour. On his way out, Paul says only: “Granted.”

At Ferréol, the slab has dried. Work resumes in January.

Q4.right: The contaminated soil is found under the slabs: the prefecture has everything dug up again, and work at Ferréol is halted for two years.
Q4.wrong: Nobody lifts the slabs. The business incubator opens in 1995, on top of 2,600 tonnes of earth that smells of diesel.

Q5.right: Marcel Roussillon resigns “for health reasons”. Superintendent Borel is transferred to Montluçon.
Q5.wrong: Marcel Roussillon is re-elected in 1995. He still wears his signet ring.

Q6.right: Marcel Chaptal will not be prosecuted for his letters. He repaints the east wall himself, in white. The foundryman doesn't come back.
Q6.wrong: The Bureau receives two more letters from the “ghost” in December. Karim keeps them in a drawer, just in case.

cases.epilogue:
The following Monday, in the Bureau's post, an unstamped envelope, left at the front desk of head office. Inside, a plain white card, without a word. Just an ink drawing, very fine: a salamander in flames. On the back, a Latin motto: Nutrisco et extinguo.

Odile looks at it for a long time. “I've seen it somewhere before.” She doesn't say where.
cases.solution: Bernard Faure was blackmailing Roger Ferrand, who was burying under new slabs the contaminated soil he was being paid to remove. On Tuesday 16 November, Faure comes to Ferréol to collect one last payment. They argue on the walkway of the forge workshop, and Ferrand pushes him. Faure survives the fall. Ferrand calls Hervé Vallenot from the watchman's hut. Vallenot arrives, sees that Faure is still breathing and refuses to call for help. He smokes four cigarillos beside him, then they stage the fall and leave. Faure dies around midnight, crawling towards the door. The next day, Marcel Roussillon has the case closed. As for the ghost's letter, it was written by Marcel Chaptal.

cases.title: The Drowned Man of the Ouvèze
cases.subtitle: A case for the Bureau of Occult Affairs
cases.intro:
Thursday 16 June 1994, fourth floor of head office, Lyon. It is already thirty degrees at ten in the morning, and Odile's fan is stirring the paperwork.

The letter came with the morning post. A sheet of squared exercise paper, a schoolgirl's handwriting, round and careful. Folded inside it, a page from Le Drômois of 2 June. In one corner of the page, dark red stains, like juice. Postmark: Nyons, Tuesday 14th.

{{d:lettre_anonyme|“Dear journalist of Occult Affairs. You write about ghosts, so come to Nyons. Look at the photo. The man on the right is Jacques Garcin. He drowned in the Ouvèze on 22 September 1992, his name is on the plaque in Vaison. Now he plays boules. Everyone here says it: the river gives back its dead. Chabert the miller swore he saw him swept away. The miller lied. Ask him why.”}}

The page is {{d:photo_concours|the winners' photo from the Grand Prix de la Digue}}, at the {{l:boulodrome|Nyons boules ground}}. Two men in vests, a cup between them. The caption says {{p:tardieu|Raoul Tardieu}} and {{p:royer|Lucien Royer}}. Royer turned his head just as the flash went off. You can see an ear, a cheek, a cap.

At eleven, Odile comes back up with a fax from the Valence office. A short item from that morning's Drômois. “Nyons: miller drowned in the canal.” {{p:chabert|Aimé Chabert}}, 63, owner of the {{l:moulin|oil mill}} in the Roman bridge quarter, was found at dawn against the canal grating. The {{l:gendarmerie|gendarmes}} have concluded it was an accident. Last line: “In 1992 Aimé Chabert witnessed the heroic death of {{p:garcin|Jacques Garcin}}, swept away by the Ouvèze flood while going to the aid of campers. {{p:helene|His widow, Hélène}}, lives in Nyons.”

Karim has read the letter three times. “She wrote on Tuesday. He died on Wednesday night.”

Jean-Loup Sarrazin puts his head round the door. “A river that gives back its dead. It's summer, people want a shiver on the beach. You leave tonight.” Paul folds the newspaper page in two without taking his eyes off the photo. “Granted.”

Three hours of motorway, then the road up the Eygues valley. It is dark when you arrive. The car windows are down, there is a smell of lime blossom and cut lavender, and the cicadas have not yet realised the sun has set. The {{l:agence|Le Drômois office}}, on avenue Henri-Rochier, used to be a haberdasher's. The metal shutter is half down. A fan turns on the ceiling, and on the desk they have left for you, someone has put a basket of apricots.
cases.briefing: Each lead you read for the first time costs a quarter of a day before Thursday's deadline, and you have 20; rereading is free. This time the calendar matters: some leads only appear from a certain day, others disappear if you take too long, because people leave and things get lost. Some people will only talk if you come back with the right piece of evidence, or the right face. When you are ready, write your article.

clues.button: Talk to Gisèle Arnaud, the correspondent
clues.title: Gisèle Arnaud, correspondent
clues.text:
{{p:gisele|Gisèle Arnaud}} has been Le Drômois's correspondent in Nyons for twenty-two years. She covers council meetings, agricultural shows, weddings and boules tournaments. She has brought a lemon cake “for the Lyon people” and she watches you eat it.

“The photo's mine. Sunday 29 May, at La Digue. It's the first time they've ever picked me up for the regional page.” She smiles, then she stops smiling. “He turned his head just as I pressed the button. I didn't do it on purpose, you have to believe me. I didn't know, about Garcin.”

Since 2 June, she says, people have talked about nothing else. In Vaison most of all. “They all lost someone, down there. And now they see their dead everywhere. {{p:rosa|Rosa Bérenger}}, one of the flood widows, swears she saw her husband last Thursday, at the market, in front of the cheese stall. She spends her days at the {{l:memorial|memorial}}, near the Roman bridge in Vaison. She says the river gives back its dead. People are starting to repeat it.”

She lowers her voice, though there is nobody else in the office. “And there's this old gentleman, at the Pension des Forts. He came in on 2 June and bought three copies of the paper. Three. He asked me exactly what time I took the photo. I told him about six. He said: no, at twelve minutes to six, look at the shadow of the plane tree.” She checked. He was right.

“His name's {{p:firmin|Achard}}, I think. He plays boules, but I've never seen him win.”
