LE DRÔMOIS, 25 SEPTEMBER 1992, PAGE 1
The hero of the Camping des Saules. Jacques Garcin, 48, born in Givors, manager of the Camping des Saules upstream of Vaison, was swept away late on Tuesday afternoon as he went back for the occupants of a caravan at the far end of the site. His friend Aimé Chabert, a miller from Nyons who had come to help with the evacuation: “I saw him go off towards the caravan at the far end. The water took him. There was nothing I could do.” His car was found at the ford, upside down. The body has not been found. (Photo: J. Garcin at the campsite reception, summer 1991.)

LE DRÔMOIS, 28 SEPTEMBER 1992, PAGE 3, LIST OF VICTIMS (EXTRACT)
… Thierry MOLLET, 26, and Nathalie BRUN, 24, from Roanne, on holiday, found at Roaix …

(Handwritten, at the bottom of the page:) In the 1991 photo he has a moustache and dark hair. The nose has been broken, and badly set. O.

clues.button: Read Odile's fax: a letter to the editor
clues.title: The miller's letter
clues.text:
On Monday morning the {{d:lettre_chabert|fax}} rings before you have finished your coffee. Odile has written across the top of the first page, in felt-tip: “Reached Valence on Friday, in the readers' letters. They put it aside. They didn't know what to do with it. I do.”

[[fax]]

Nobody says anything for a while. The fan turns. Karim rereads the last sentence under his breath.

Paul lights his cigarette, for once, and leaves it to burn down in the ashtray without touching it.

facts.text: Posted in Valence by Aimé Chabert on Wednesday 15 June, the day he died. He admits he lied in 1992 and says he will speak to the gendarmes on Thursday.
“I lied in 1992. Jacques is not dead. I will tell the gendarmes on Thursday.”
facts.label: His letter

facts.text: “Hélène knows, I told her on Sunday.” She knew the miller would talk on Thursday.
facts.label: According to Chabert

clues.fax:
AIMÉ CHABERT · MOULIN CHABERT · QUARTIER DU PONT ROMAN · 26110 NYONS
TO THE EDITORS OF LE DRÔMOIS, VALENCE · POSTED 15 JUNE 1994

Dear Sirs,

On 2 June you published the photo of a man called Lucien Royer. He is Jacques Garcin. He did not die in 1992. I lied to the gendarmes. I did not see him swept away. I found him alive, that night, up in the hills, and he asked me to say he was dead. I did. He did not go back for the caravan at the far end. He had forgotten it.

I will tell the gendarmes on Thursday. I am also writing to the paper, because it was the paper that made him a hero, and because I am afraid I will not have the courage on Thursday.

Hélène knows. I told her on Sunday. She asked me to wait. I will not wait any longer.

If anything happens to me, it will not be the river.

Aimé Chabert

clues.button: Bring in the four witnesses from Wednesday night
clues.title: Karim's grid
clues.text:
Paul has asked Gisèle to lend you the back room of the office, where the old issues are kept. A table, four chairs, stacks of yellowed newspapers up to the ceiling. He has them come in one at a time, an hour apart, without telling them who else is coming. Karim writes everything down, word for word, on a large sketch pad.

{{p:helene|Hélène Garcin}} comes in a pale suit, her handbag on her knees, and does not sit back in the chair. {{p:royer|Lucien Royer}} comes because Tardieu told him to, cap in hand, and watches the door. {{p:firmin|Firmin Achard}} arrives exactly on time, and points it out. {{p:sandrine|Sandrine Mollet}} comes between two days of picking, her fingers red, and answers the table rather than Paul.

Paul asks them all the same question: on Wednesday night, at about ten, where were you, what did you have on you, and why were you out?

On her way out, Sandrine turns back to Karim, not to Paul. “The man I gave the boule back to, at twenty to, under the street lamp at La Digue. I'd watched him play all afternoon, from a distance. Short hair, grey. High forehead, with lines, three of them. A moustache, I think. Well. I don't know any more. I've looked at that man so much in the paper. Square chin. I didn't look him in the eye.”

Karim has made a fair copy of the statements, next to what the gendarmes' file says. He has drawn the grids. “One of them is lying. Everything he says is false. The other three are telling the truth.”

facts.text: Describes the man she gave the boule back to, on Wednesday at 10.40 p.m.: short grey hair, high lined forehead, “a moustache, I think”, square chin. She had watched him play in daylight.
facts.label: The description

clues.button: Put together the identikit portrait with Yves
clues.title: The identikit portrait
clues.text:
Yves has taken an old identikit kit out of a suitcase, bought at a police sale in 1981: sheets of features printed on tracing paper, which you lay one over another. He spreads them out on the desk, under the fan, and puts a stapler on each pile so they don't blow away.

“Two witnesses. Sandrine saw him play in broad daylight, from a distance, and in the evening under a street lamp. Karim saw him from a metre away, by candlelight, frightened. Each of them gets something wrong. People always get something wrong. You just have to know what, and why.”

He hands you the overlays.

clues.title: Warrant Officer Montagne
clues.text:
Warrant Officer {{p:montagne|Montagne}} receives you standing, behind the station counter, the way you receive people who have come to report a stolen bicycle. He has a moustache trimmed to the millimetre and a mug that says “Club taurin de Nyons”.

“The Bureau of Occult Affairs.” He says it slowly, so you can hear how it sounds. “A man of sixty-three who drinks, who lives alone, who goes out by his canal at midnight and falls in. 1.8 grams. There's nothing occult about that. Full stop.”

A toxicology test? “What for? We know what he drank: marc. The bottle was on the table.” Nobody pushed him, he says, there's not a sign of a struggle, not one witness. The ghost? “That's for your paper. I don't have a ghost column.”

He sees you out. On the doorstep, he adds all the same, in an undertone: “The death was certified by {{p:sauvan|Dr Sauvan}}. She asks questions too. She's young.”

facts.text: Concludes it was an accident: 1.8 g of alcohol, a fall into the canal. No toxicology test. “Nobody pushed him.”
Accidental death: drunk, he fell into the canal going out through the millrace door.
facts.label: According to the gendarmes

facts.text: Certified Aimé Chabert's death. “She asks questions,” according to the warrant officer.

clues.speaker: montagne

clues.button: Read the file, since there's nothing to hide
clues.title: The gendarmerie file
clues.text:
“You want to read the file? Read it. There's nothing to hide, it's an accident.” The warrant officer sets you up in an empty office with a cardboard folder and shuts the door behind you. It runs to only nine pages.

The {{d:pv|report}} is dated Thursday 16 June, 6.30 a.m. The body was found at 5.10 a.m. by {{p:isnard|the canal keeper}}, against the grating, two hundred metres downstream of the mill. Death certified by {{p:sauvan|Dr Sauvan}}. At the mill, the street door was locked. Chabert's bunch of keys was hanging on its nail, inside. The door onto the millrace was open, and so was the sluice gate: “the victim must have opened it himself, while intoxicated”. Nobody pushed him, the officer concludes. On the bank of the {{l:canal|canal}}, upstream, a metal {{d:lampe|torch}}, still switched on, the battery almost flat. On the handle, a Dymo label: “CAMPING DES SAULES · ACCUEIL”.

The house-to-house inquiry fits on one page. Four people out on Wednesday at about 10 p.m.: {{p:helene|Mme Hélène Garcin}}, at the {{l:arcades|Café des Arcades}}; “a man with boules”, whose name nobody knows; “the old gentleman from the pension”, {{p:firmin|M. Achard}}; and “a seasonal worker”, {{p:sandrine|Sandrine Mollet}}, who is staying at the {{l:camping_municipal|municipal campsite}}.

And four statements taken, three lines each:
{{p:gaston|Gaston Rey}}, road mender: at about 10 p.m., a woman alone near the La Digue boules ground.
{{p:fredo|The waiter at the Arcades}}: his 10 p.m. customer “watched the door all evening”.
{{p:josiane|Josiane Pellegrin}}, cleaning lady: M. Chabert told her on Wednesday that he had to “have it out with someone, at the canal, tonight”.
And the torch, found on the bank: whoever was holding it was at the canal.

Nobody made the connection between the torch and the {{l:camping_saules|Camping des Saules}}. Or nobody wanted to.

facts.text: Mill door locked, Chabert's key ring on its nail inside, millrace door open, sluice gate opened “by the victim”. Body found at 5.10 a.m. against the grating.
Found switched on, on the bank of the canal upstream of the mill. Dymo label: “CAMPING DES SAULES · ACCUEIL”. Whoever was holding it was at the canal.
At the Café des Arcades around 10 p.m., according to the door-to-door inquiries.
facts.label: Wednesday night

facts.text: Around 10 p.m. on Wednesday, saw a woman on her own near La Digue boules ground.
Her 10 p.m. customer at the Arcades “watched the door all evening”: she was waiting for someone.
On Wednesday Chabert told her he had to “have it out with someone, at the canal, tonight”.
Seasonal worker, staying at the municipal campsite. Out on Wednesday around 10 p.m.
Out around 10 p.m., according to the door-to-door inquiries.
facts.label: Wednesday night

clues.title: Dr Sauvan
clues.text:
{{p:sauvan|Dr Anne Sauvan}}'s surgery is on the first floor, above a shop selling Provençal fabrics. She is thirty-two, her hair held up with a pencil, and between patients she smokes at the window, blowing the smoke outside as if that way it didn't count.

“I don't sign what I don't know. I wrote drowning. I wrote alcohol. I didn't write accident, the gendarme wrote that.” She draws on her cigarette. “Death was between eleven at night and one in the morning. Not before eleven, that much I'll sign.”

What bothers her is the hands. “A drowning man struggles. He grabs at the weeds, he breaks his nails on the concrete, he's covered in silt. Him, nothing. Clean hands. Not a scratch. He didn't fight.” She stubs the cigarette out on the sill. “He was asleep when he went into the water. A man who's drunk a litre of marc can sleep, fine. But not that deeply.”

The warrant officer didn't want any tests. She kept a tube of blood in the fridge and on Friday she sent it to a laboratory in Lyon, at her own expense. “The result comes Tuesday. Come back Tuesday. And don't tell Montagne, he'd be put out.”

facts.text: Aimé Chabert died between 11 p.m. and 1 a.m., not before 11 p.m. No sign of a struggle: “He was asleep when he went into the water.”
Died after 11 p.m., without struggling. Dr Sauvan has had his blood tested in Lyon: result on Tuesday 21.
facts.label: According to Dr Sauvan

clues.speaker: sauvan

clues.button: Call Dr Sauvan back about the test
clues.title: The laboratory report
clues.text:
Dr Sauvan has the laboratory's sheet in her hand when you come in. She doesn't ask you to sit down.

{{d:analyse|Test report}}, Mérieux laboratory, Lyon. Blood alcohol: 1.8 g. And one more line: nitrazepam, at a concentration “consistent with several tablets taken in the hours preceding death”.

“Mogadon. A sleeping pill. It gets prescribed to insomniacs, to widows, to people who are frightened at night. With a litre of marc on top, he couldn't have lifted an arm.” She folds the sheet. “He didn't take it, I've been his doctor for four years. Someone gave it to him.”

She doesn't need to be asked the next question. “In the centre there's only one chemist that dispenses a lot of it. The {{l:pharmacie|Pharmacie du Pont}}. {{p:roux|Mme Roux}}. She won't tell you anything. Well, she'll tell you she never tells anyone anything, and then she'll talk.”

She is taking the report to the gendarmerie this afternoon. “Montagne will be put out. Too bad.”

facts.text: Aimé Chabert's blood: 1.8 g of alcohol and a heavy dose of nitrazepam (Mogadon), taken a few hours before death.
Drugged with Mogadon before he went into the water. He didn't take it.
facts.label: The laboratory

clues.title: Mme Roux, chemist
clues.text:
{{p:roux|Mme Roux}} wears a starched white coat and glasses on a chain. Behind her, earthenware jars and a poster warning against sunburn.

“I don't discuss my customers. Ever.” She puts three boxes away on a shelf, very carefully. “Mogadon, I dispense it to about twenty people. Elderly people, mostly. And people who've had a misfortune.”

She turns towards the shop window. “Only one of those people came in last Thursday, at half past eight, before I'd even raised the blind. To renew her prescription, ten days early. She told me she'd tipped the box into the sink. I told her it didn't matter.” For a moment she says nothing. “She had a great misfortune, in 1992. I haven't told you her name.”

She doesn't need to. There is only one widow of 1992 in Nyons whom people call “her”, lowering their voices.

facts.text: A customer, widowed in 1992, came in on Thursday 16 June at 8.30 a.m. to renew her Mogadon ten days early: “I tipped the box into the sink.”
According to the chemist, renewed her Mogadon early on the morning of Thursday 16, the day after the miller died.
facts.label: The Mogadon

clues.speaker: roux

clues.button: Meet the man from the Mutuelle
clues.title: Jean-Claude Vasseur, of the Mutuelle rhodanienne
clues.text:
{{p:vasseur|Jean-Claude Vasseur}}, claims inspector for the Mutuelle rhodanienne, has the best table on the terrace of the Hôtel de la Place, under the only parasol still standing. Grey suit, tie loosened by two centimetres, a solar calculator on top of his files.

“The Bureau of Occult Affairs. I was told.” He orders two mint diabolos without asking you. “Me, I'm the Bureau of Very Concrete Affairs.”

The contract is simple, he says. {{d:assurance|Life insurance}} on Jacques Garcin, taken out in 1988. Declaratory judgment of death in July 1993, in Carpentras. 1.4 million francs paid to the widow in December. “She bought back her parents' house, rue des Grands-Forts. She invested the rest for the children's education. A very sensible woman.”

“If Garcin is alive, it all goes back to the Mutuelle. All of it. The house, the investments. And if the widow knew he was alive, it's no longer a repayment, it's fraud. The criminal court.” He taps the calculator. “Prison, possibly.”

He was sent after the photo of 2 June, when someone telephoned his Avignon office. A young woman's voice, who didn't give her name. And there is something else. “The miller called me himself, on Tuesday the 14th. He wanted to know what a witness who'd made a false statement was facing. I told him to come and see me. He was supposed to come on Thursday.” He sighs. “If you want my opinion, I think he was blackmailing the widow. A poor devil with debts and a secret. We see them every day.”

facts.text: Jacques Garcin's life insurance: 1.4 million francs paid to Hélène in December 1993. If Garcin is alive, it must all be repaid; if the widow knew, it is fraud.
Inspector for the Mutuelle rhodanienne, in Nyons since the photo of 2 June. An anonymous young woman called his office.
Called the Mutuelle on Tuesday 14 to ask what a false witness was facing. Was due to come in on the Thursday. Vasseur suspects him of blackmailing the widow.
facts.label: According to Vasseur

clues.speaker: vasseur

clues.title: Fredo, waiter at the Arcades
clues.text:
{{p:fredo|Fredo}} is wiping the terrace tables under the arcades with a cloth that has seen better days. He is on first-name terms with everyone, Paul included.

“Mme Garcin? Wednesday, yeah. She sat there, half past nine, at the corner table. A mint cordial. She was watching the door. Not the square, the door. Every time somebody came in, she looked up.” He folds the cloth in four. “She was waiting for someone, no question. Someone who never showed.”

She left at a quarter to eleven. “I remember because she hadn't finished her drink, and she left a twenty for a mint cordial. She went that way.” He points to the street that runs down to the east. “Towards the Roman bridge. Not towards home. Home's up the top, in Les Forts.”

“The old boy from the pension, M. Achard, he reads his paper on the {{l:pont|Roman bridge}} every night, from nine till all hours. You could set your watch by him. Wednesday, same.”

facts.text: Hélène Garcin at the Arcades from 9.30 p.m. to 10.45 p.m., a mint cordial, eyes on the door. Left without finishing her drink, towards the Roman bridge, not towards home.
facts.label: Wednesday night

facts.text: Left the Arcades at 10.45 p.m., heading for the Roman bridge.
facts.label: According to Fredo

facts.text: Reads his paper on the Roman bridge every night, from 9 p.m. “till all hours”. Wednesday too.
facts.label: According to Fredo

clues.speaker: fredo

clues.title: Hélène Garcin, the widow
clues.text:
The house is at the top of Les Forts, rue des Grands-Forts, where the lanes turn into covered stairways. Blue shutters, a bay tree in a pot, a teenager's bike against the wall. {{p:helene|Hélène Garcin}} opens the door before you have knocked. She saw you coming up.

She serves you cold water in stemmed glasses, on a tray. She is very calm. She talks about Nyons olive oil, the only one in France with an appellation, about last winter's harvest, about the price per litre. When Paul lays the competition page on the table, she doesn't look at it.

“Jacques is dead, monsieur. The river gives nothing back. I know, I waited three weeks by the water for it to give him back to me.” She puts her glass down. “I've stopped the subscription to Le Drômois. The children don't need to see that.”

Wednesday night? She was at the Arcades. “I was waiting for a friend, who didn't come. I went home.” She has worked in the mill shop since last year: “Aimé offered it to me. He was good to us.” The keys to the mill? “I gave them back to him in May. The shop closes in summer, we only press in winter.”

As she sees you out, she adds, in the same tone: “A gentleman from the Mutuelle came to see me. He's staying at the {{l:hotel|Hôtel de la Place}}. {{p:vasseur|M. Vasseur}}. You should talk to each other, you'd get on.”

facts.text: “Jacques is dead. The river gives nothing back.” Stopped her subscription to Le Drômois after the photo.
Says she waited at the Arcades for “a friend who didn't come”, then went home.
facts.label: Wednesday night

facts.text: Says she gave the mill keys back to Aimé Chabert in May. Has worked in the mill shop since 1993.
facts.label: The keys

facts.text: Inspector for the Mutuelle, staying at the Hôtel de la Place. Came to see Hélène.

clues.speaker: helene

clues.button: Come back while Hélène is at the shop
clues.title: The Garcin house
clues.text:
You come back the next day, at the hour when Hélène minds the oil shop in the covered market. It is {{p:helene|her son}} Julien who opens the door, sixteen, a Walkman round his neck. He says his mother isn't in. Paul says he knows. Julien hesitates, then steps aside. “You're the ones from the paper. About my father.” It isn't a question.

He shows you the back bedroom, his father's. Everything has been left as it was at the campsite: the map of the Ouvèze valley pinned to the wall, a pétanque cup, the wedding photo. “Mum doesn't want anyone touching it. She goes in there in the evenings. She shuts the door.”

In the sitting room the bureau isn't locked. The letter from the Mutuelle rhodanienne, December 1993: payment of 1,400,000 francs under the {{d:assurance|life insurance}} policy. And under the letter, a Post Office counterfoil book. {{d:mandats|Postal orders}}, one a month, on the 5th, since 5 November 1992. 1,500 francs each time. Payee: “L. Royer, poste restante, 26170 Buis-les-Baronnies”. The last counterfoils are from May and June 1994.

Julien has stayed in the doorway. “Who's Royer?” Nobody answers him. He puts his headphones back over his ears without switching the music on.

facts.text: Letter from the Mutuelle, December 1993: 1,400,000 F paid to Hélène Garcin. Kept in the bureau.
facts.label: The letter

facts.text: Postal order counterfoils: 1,500 F on the 5th of every month since November 1992, to “L. Royer, poste restante, Buis-les-Baronnies”. In Hélène's bureau.
Has sent 1,500 F a month to “L. Royer” since November 1992, two months after the flood.
facts.label: The postal orders

clues.button: Go back to Hélène with the time she left
clues.title: Hélène, second interview
clues.text:
This time Hélène sees you in the kitchen, with no tray. Paul lays the times on the table one by one, like playing cards. The Arcades left at a quarter to eleven, towards the bridge. The sluice gate opened with a key.

She doesn't deny it for long. She corrects herself. “I went to the mill, yes. I wanted to talk to Aimé. He hadn't come to the Arcades. The door was locked, he didn't answer. I left.” She has the keys to the shop, yes. “I didn't give them back. I lied to you because I knew what you'd think.”

“What did you want to talk to him about?” She looks at the window, where you can see, very far off, the line of the valley. “About my husband.”

She doesn't ask what you know. She doesn't ask whether she is under suspicion. All she asks, at the end, is whether the children will hear about what is written on Saturday.

facts.text: Admits she went to the mill around 11 p.m. “to talk to Aimé”, and that she still has the shop keys. Says the door was locked and she left.
facts.label: Second interview

clues.speaker: helene
clues.buttonAlone: Question Hélène Garcin about the time she left
clues.titleAlone: Hélène Garcin, faced with the time

clues.title: Firmin Achard
clues.text:
The Pension des Forts has six rooms and a terrace under a vine trellis. {{p:firmin|Firmin Achard}} has been settled there since 30 May, at the table at the back, a leather bag at his feet with three pétanque boules in it. White shirt buttoned to the collar despite the heat, a Drômois folded on the table, a pipe gone out.

He accepts the pastis. He looks at you one by one, Paul, Yves, Karim, the way you look at boules before choosing which one to play.

“I take the evening air on the bridge, like every old man in France.” Wednesday? “From four minutes to nine until ten past midnight.” He saw nothing. “I saw the water. It was low. It's always low in June, here.” He speaks of the river as of someone he has known a long time and slightly mistrusts.

Karim asks him if he believes in ghosts. Firmin looks at him for a long while. “I believe in people who come back. It's not the same thing.”

He leaves on Tuesday, he says. He has his room until Monday night. “After that, you know where to find me.” Nobody does.

facts.text: In Nyons since 30 May, at the Pension des Forts. Says he took the evening air on the Roman bridge on Wednesday from 8.56 p.m. to 12.10 a.m., and saw nothing “but the water”.
Leaves Nyons on the morning of Tuesday 21 June.
facts.label: His departure

clues.speaker: firmin

clues.button: Open the envelope left by M. Achard
clues.title: Firmin Achard's notes
clues.text:
The landlady of the pension stops you on the stairs. “M. Achard left this morning, at six, with his bag. He's paid till the end of the month. He left this for you. He said: for the journalists from Lyon, they'll come on Tuesday.” She holds out a large brown envelope, sealed with wax.

Inside, a {{d:carnet_firmin|notebook}} bound in black cloth. On the first page, a very old stamp in red ink: a salamander in flames. And below it, in fountain pen: “The ghost of the Ouvèze. Opened 30 May 1994.”

The handwriting is fine, slanting, as regular as a musical score. Every line begins with a time.

“2 June. The photo. It isn't a dead man. It's a living man who turned his head.”
“11 June. A young woman comes out of the mill in tears. The miller stays a long time on the footbridge.”
“15 June. 9.41 p.m. The widow sits down at the Arcades. 9.58 p.m. The miller comes out by the millrace door and walks upstream. 10.05 p.m. Two men on the bank, a torch. The miller is crying. 10.32 p.m. The man with the boules sees me. He drops the torch, which stays on in the grass, and runs off towards La Digue. 10.50 p.m. The miller goes back into the mill by the millrace. 11.05 p.m. A woman goes in by the little street door, with a key. The widow. 11.12 p.m. The sluice gate roars, the millrace fills. 11.27 p.m. She comes out alone, locks the door, stays at the parapet. She is not crying. The miller does not come out.”
“16 June. There is no ghost in Nyons. There is a widow.”

The last page is blank, except for one line: “What you do with this is no concern of ours.”

facts.text: Firmin Achard's notebook, a salamander in flames on the first page. Records the night of 15 June minute by minute, from the Roman bridge.
Goes into the mill by the little door at 11.05 p.m., with a key. The sluice gate roars at 11.12 p.m. Comes out alone at 11.27 p.m. and locks the door.
facts.label: According to Firmin

facts.text: On the bank with the miller from 10.05 p.m. to 10.32 p.m., then runs off, dropping the torch. The miller goes back into the mill alive at 10.50 p.m.
facts.label: According to Firmin

facts.text: Had been watching the mill since 30 May. Saw everything on 15 June and told no one. “What you do with this is no concern of ours.”
facts.label: The notebook

clues.button: Talk to Josiane, the cleaning lady
clues.title: Josiane Pellegrin, cleaning lady
clues.text:
{{p:josiane|Josiane Pellegrin}} still comes to the mill every morning to water the geraniums in the yard. “Nobody else is going to.” She is seventy, wears a flowered apron, and calls the dead man “Monsieur Aimé”.

On Wednesday he was “all out of sorts”. He told her he had to have it out with someone, at the canal, that evening. “He never said who. He said: Josiane, tomorrow I'm going to do something I should've done two years ago.”

On Thursday morning, once the gendarmes had gone, she went in. “The two marc glasses, on the draining board, rinsed, turned upside down. Monsieur Aimé never rinsed a glass in his life. Never. I'd been rinsing them for him for thirty years.” She told the gendarmes. The warrant officer wrote down “two glasses”.

And the Saturday before, the 11th, a young woman came. “A seasonal girl, fingers red from the cherries. She was shouting in the yard, shoving a newspaper under his nose. She was saying: did you watch him die? Did you watch? Monsieur Aimé never answered.” She crosses herself. “Her name's {{p:sandrine|Mollet}}, I think. She said her name as she left, like throwing something down.”

The keys? “Mme Hélène's got her key to the shop, of course she has, she works there. She's always had it.”

facts.text: Thursday morning, two marc glasses rinsed and turned upside down on the draining board. “Monsieur Aimé never rinsed a glass in his life.” Someone drank with him.
facts.label: The glasses

facts.text: According to her, Hélène still has her key to the mill shop.
facts.label: The keys

facts.text: Came shouting at the mill on Saturday 11 June, a newspaper in her hand: “Did you watch him die?”
facts.label: According to Josiane

facts.text: Wednesday: “Tomorrow I'm going to do something I should've done two years ago.”
facts.label: According to Josiane

clues.speaker: josiane

clues.title: Chabert's mill
clues.text:
Chabert's mill is a big stone building on the edge of the canal, with a wheel that has stopped turning and a shop closed behind a shutter. Josiane opens up the millstone room for you. It is as cool as a cellar, and it smells of last winter's crushed olives and wet stone.

On the table, the bottle of marc is still there, three-quarters empty. The nail for the key ring, near the little street door. At the far end, the millrace door opens onto a plank footbridge over the water. Next to it, the big iron wheel of the sluice gate, and a chain with a brass padlock, snapped shut.

In the office, the wastepaper basket hasn't been emptied. Yves pulls out a sheet torn in two, then crumpled. The handwriting shakes. {{d:brouillon|“To the gendarmes. In September 1992, I lied. Jacques Garcin was not swept away by the water. I found him that night, up in the hills, alive, and he asked me to say he was dead. I did it because he was my friend and because he had already had enough”}} The sentence stops there.

On the footbridge, Karim leans over the millrace. The water is black and fast, and it makes almost no sound.

facts.text: Torn draft found in the miller's wastepaper basket: “In September 1992, I lied. Jacques Garcin was not swept away. I found him alive, and he asked me to say he was dead.”
The little street door, the nail for the key ring, the millrace door, the footbridge, and the sluice gate locked with a brass padlock.

clues.title: Norbert Isnard, canal keeper
clues.text:
{{p:isnard|Norbert Isnard}} has been keeper of the canal since 1961. He is the one who opens and closes the sluices, who shares out the water to the gardens by day and hour, and who clears the grating in the mornings of branches, dead cats and, once in thirty-three years, a man. He talks in litres per second.

“The mill's sluice gate, in June, it's shut. Nobody presses in June.” On Wednesday, at 11.10 p.m., the level at the divider downstream dropped four centimetres in one go. He shows you the paper roll from his water-level recorder, a line of blue ink with a step in it. “Somebody opened the mill gate. The water rushed into the millrace. There's a real current in there when it's open. A man falls in, he doesn't come up.”

The padlock? Snapped shut on the chain, in the open position. “The gendarmes say it was Aimé, drunk. But that padlock doesn't close without the key, it's the association's model. And Aimé's key ring was on its nail, inside, the gendarmes wrote it down.” He shrugs. “So somebody can tell me with what key.”

There are only two, he says. “Mine, right here.” He shows it, hanging round his neck on a bootlace. “And the one on the mill key ring. Which has a copy, in the shop, for when Aimé wasn't there.”

facts.text: The mill's sluice gate was opened on Wednesday around 11.10 p.m.: the canal level dropped 4 cm in one go. The padlock was closed again, which takes a key.
facts.label: The sluice gate

facts.text: Only two keys: his own, which he wears round his neck, and the one on the mill key ring, a copy of which is kept in the shop.
facts.label: The keys

facts.text: His key ring was on its nail, inside: he could not have closed the sluice gate padlock himself.
facts.label: According to Isnard

clues.speaker: isnard

clues.title: The canal bank
clues.text:
The grass on the bank, upstream of the mill, has been flattened over a square metre, and it hasn't sprung back. Yves photographs two kinds of footprint in the dry earth at the edge: town shoes, resoled, and heavy-cleated work boots.

Paul turns round. From here you can see everything: the canal all the way to the mill, the millrace footbridge, the little street door. And above, the humpback of the {{l:pont|Roman bridge}}, its stone parapet, the outline of a street lamp. “Someone up there sees everything. And nobody sees him, with the light behind him.”

facts.text: Flattened grass where the torch was found: two men, town shoes and work boots. The Roman bridge overlooks the whole scene.
facts.label: The bank

clues.title: The Roman bridge
clues.text:
The Roman bridge spans the Eygues in a single arch, so high it feels like climbing a hill. From the top you can see the canal, the mill, La Digue, and the whole old town rising in tiers.

On the parapet, where the stone is most worn, a small heap of pipe ash the wind hasn't yet carried off. Wedged in a crack, a Drômois from Wednesday 15 June, folded in four, the boules page on top.

And carved into the soft stone with the point of a knife, so small you have to lean in: a lizard in flames. The lines are fresh. The stone dust is still white in the grooves.

Karim runs his finger over it. “We've seen that before.” Paul doesn't answer. He is looking down at the mill. From here, you see the little street door as if you were standing in front of it.

facts.text: Pipe ash and a copy of Le Drômois from 15 June on the parapet. A salamander in flames carved with a knife, quite fresh. You can see the little door of the mill as if you were standing in front of it.
Someone smoked a pipe and read the paper of 15 June on the bridge. And carved a salamander into the stone.
facts.label: The bridge

clues.title: Gaston Rey, road mender
clues.text:
{{p:gaston|Gaston Rey}} is the town's road mender and secretary of la Boule nyonsaise, which amounts to spending his days at La Digue, between the plane trees and the rake. He tells everything like a game: who pointed, who shot, who hit a carreau.

“Royer? Lucien, from Les Pilles. He works for Tardieu, at the {{l:ferme_tardieu|farm}}, above the road. He plays all right, but he shoots lyonnaise style, arms out straight, three steps of run-up. You can tell he's not from round here. Some evenings he comes on his own with big boules, proper lyonnaise ones, bronze, and he plays against nobody.”

He has seen the photo. “Everyone says it's Garcin. I say Garcin played pétanque like everybody else.” He thinks about it. “Mind you. Garcin was from Givors.”

On Wednesday, around ten, while locking up the club hut, he saw a {{p:sandrine|woman}} alone on the ground, searching the earth by the light of a lighter. “A young one, a cherry picker. I asked her if she'd lost something. She said yes, without saying what.”

facts.text: Royer works for Tardieu, at Les Pilles. Shoots “lyonnaise style”. Sometimes comes alone in the evening to play with bronze lyonnaise boules.
facts.label: Royer

facts.text: Plays lyonnaise, a game from the Lyon region. Garcin was from Givors.
facts.label: His boules

facts.text: Wednesday around 10 p.m., alone on La Digue boules ground, looking for something on the ground by the light of a lighter.
facts.label: According to Gaston

clues.speaker: gaston

clues.button: Look at the tournament entry sheet
clues.title: The Grand Prix sheet
clues.text:
Gaston brings a ring binder out of the club hut. The {{d:feuille_concours|entry sheet}} for Le Grand Prix de la Digue, Sunday 29 May, thirty-two doubles teams. Each player has written his name in his own hand.

Team no. 23. “TARDIEU Raoul”, in slanting capitals. And next to it, in another hand: two letters, “Ga”, crossed out with a stroke pressed so hard it has torn through the paper. Then, straight after: “ROYER L.”

Gaston had never noticed. “He started writing something else. Like when you sign a cheque with your wife's name.”

facts.text: Entry sheet of 29 May, team no. 23: Royer first wrote “Ga”, crossed it out, then wrote “ROYER L.”
Started to sign “Ga”, then corrected himself.
facts.label: The sheet

clues.title: Sandrine Mollet, cherry picker
clues.text:
The municipal campsite lies on the bank of the Eygues, under the poplars. In June it is the seasonal workers' campsite: ridge tents, Renault 4s, washing lines strung between the trees. {{p:sandrine|Sandrine Mollet}} comes back from picking at four o'clock, an empty crate on her shoulder. She is twenty-four and red-fingered up to the wrists.

“I do the cherries. Then the apricots. Then the lavender. I do the seasons.” She is from Roanne. She never looks anyone in the face. She talks to the crate, to the tent, to the poplar.

On Wednesday evening she was on La Digue. “I'd lost my watch in the afternoon. I went back to look for it. Didn't find it.” She found a boule instead, “a big one, not a pétanque boule”. She shrugs. “People lose things.”

When Karim asks her whether she knew Aimé Chabert, she goes into her tent and zips it shut. From inside, she says: “None of your business.”

facts.text: Seasonal worker from Roanne, 24. “I do the seasons.” Fingers red with cherry juice, like the stains on the page sent to the Bureau.
On La Digue, looking for the watch she lost in the afternoon. Found a big boule instead.
facts.label: Wednesday evening

clues.speaker: sandrine

clues.button: Take a look in Sandrine's tent
clues.title: Sandrine's tent
clues.text:
Sandrine is in the orchards. The tent isn't zipped, only tied. Paul doesn't say to go in. He doesn't say not to.

Inside, a sleeping bag, a head torch, magazines. Pinned to the canvas above the pillow, a photo cut out of a 1992 newspaper: Jacques Garcin, moustache, the caption “The hero of Camping des Saules”. The eyes have been scratched out with a knife, right through the paper.

On the crate that serves as a table, a pad of squared paper and a ballpoint pen. A torn-off sheet reading, in a round hand: “Chabert, mill, Saturday”. And a cardboard watch box, empty. On the lid, in felt-tip: “Thierry, 20”.

Yves looks at the photo with the scratched-out eyes longer than at the rest. He does not photograph it.

facts.text: The 1992 photo of Garcin pinned above her bed, the eyes scratched out with a knife. A note: “Chabert, mill, Saturday”.
facts.label: Her tent

facts.text: A pad of squared paper and a ballpoint pen, as for the anonymous letter. An empty watch box marked “Thierry, 20”.
facts.label: The paper

clues.button: Go back to Sandrine about Thierry Mollet
clues.title: Sandrine, second interview
clues.text:
Sandrine is sitting on the crate in front of the tent, and she is waiting for you. She understood when she saw Paul coming. For the first time, she looks him in the face.

“Thierry was my brother.” She says it without crying. She must have said it often in her head. “The watch was his, for his twentieth. I lost it Wednesday, on La Digue, watching him play. Him.” She doesn't say Garcin. She says him.

She recognised Garcin in the photo of 2 June. “Twenty months I've been looking at his face every night. The hero who died trying to save my brother.” She went to see Chabert on the Saturday. She shouted. He said nothing, “but he cried, and a man who's told the truth doesn't cry”. And she was the one who wrote to the Bureau. “The gendarmes would've thought I was mad. You lot, ghosts are your job.”

From her purse she takes a {{d:carte_thierry|postcard}} worn at the corners. The Roman bridge at Vaison. On the back, Thierry's handwriting, dated 21 September 1992: “Got in late. We're right at the back, under the willows, nice and quiet. The owner's friendly, he said we'd do the registration tomorrow. Love to Mum.”

“He never registered them. He evacuated with the list. They weren't on the list.” She puts the card away. “I wanted him to tell the truth, the miller. Not to die.”

facts.text: Sister of Thierry Mollet, who died in the flood. Recognised Garcin in the photo, went to see Chabert on Saturday 11, and wrote the anonymous letter to the Bureau.
facts.label: Second interview

facts.text: Thierry Mollet's postcard, 21 September 1992: “We're right at the back, under the willows. The owner said we'd do the registration tomorrow.” The caravan was not on the list.
According to Sandrine, he had not registered Thierry and Nathalie's caravan. He evacuated the campsite using the list.
facts.label: The night of the flood

clues.speaker: sandrine
clues.buttonAlone: Talk to Sandrine about Thierry Mollet

clues.title: Raoul Tardieu, fruit grower
clues.text:
The Tardieu farm stands on the way out of Les Pilles, above the road, among rows of cherry and apricot trees packed tight as soldiers. {{p:tardieu|Raoul Tardieu}} is sorting cherries under a corrugated-iron shed, a radio set on a crate. He complains about everything: the hail in May, the prices at Rungis, the seasonal workers who leave after three days.

“Lucien? He's the only one who stays.” Royer arrived in March 1993, on foot, with a bag. He asked for work. Tardieu pays him cash. “Papers, I didn't ask him for any, and he didn't offer. A good worker doesn't talk to you about his papers.” He sleeps in the {{l:ferme_tardieu|hut}} at the far end of the orchard.

Wednesday evening? “He went off about nine on the moped. He came back at eleven, I heard the engine, I wasn't asleep, my back's bad.” Eleven on the dot? “The radio news was starting.”

In the evenings Lucien often heads off towards Vaison. “To {{l:camping_saules|Camping des Saules}}, so I'm told, the one that got swept away. There's nothing left there. I never asked him what he does there.”

Walking you back to the car, he spits on the ground. “The photo, I'm the one who entered him for the tournament. He didn't want to. He really didn't want to.”

facts.text: Has employed Royer since March 1993, paid in cash, no papers. Entered him for the Grand Prix “when he really didn't want to”.
According to Tardieu, left Les Pilles on his moped around 9 p.m., back at 11 p.m. on the dot (the radio news was starting).
facts.label: Wednesday evening

facts.text: Often goes off in the evening towards Vaison, to Camping des Saules, in ruins since the flood.
facts.label: In the evenings

clues.speaker: tardieu

clues.title: Lucien Royer
clues.text:
{{p:royer|Lucien Royer}} is pruning an apricot tree at the end of a row, and doesn't turn round as you approach. Canvas cap, open shirt, a labourer's forearms. When he finally turns, he keeps the cap pulled low over his eyes and the sun at his back.

“My name's Royer. Lucien. I'm from Givors.” He says it like a lesson. The photo? “Don't like photos.” The canal? “Never set foot there. I'm not from the town, me.” On Wednesday evening he went down to Nyons to fetch a boule he'd left on La Digue that afternoon. “A lyonnaise. They cost money. Nothing else.”

He says little. He calls Tardieu's children “les gones”, the way they do in Lyon.

Paul asks him if he has any family. Royer looks at the apricot tree. “Not any more.” Then he climbs back up his stepladder.

facts.text: “My name's Royer. Lucien. I'm from Givors.” Calls children “les gones”, as in Lyon. “Family? Not any more.”
Says he never set foot at the canal, and only went down to La Digue to fetch a boule he had left there.
facts.label: Wednesday evening

clues.speaker: royer

clues.button: Go back to Royer with Karim's grid
clues.title: Royer, second interview
clues.text:
Paul lays Karim's grid on the bonnet of the car, at the end of the row of apricot trees. He says nothing. He waits.

Royer looks for a long time at the little crosses and the little circles. Then he takes off his gloves. “I was at the canal.” He sits down on the step of the stepladder. “Aimé wanted to tell the gendarmes everything, the next day. He'd told me to meet him there, on the bank, at ten. I'd brought the torch.” He says Aimé. He doesn't say Chabert, or the miller.

“I asked him to wait. Just a bit. Better I went myself. He was crying. He said he couldn't go on. He said he'd always protected me, and it was killing him.”

At half past ten he saw someone on the Roman bridge, a figure, standing still, watching. “I got scared. I dropped the torch and ran. I went to get my boule on La Digue, a girl gave it back to me. Then I went home.”

He looks up. “When I left, he was alive. He was crying, sitting in the grass. I swear it on the heads of my gones.” He stops dead. He said my.

facts.text: Was at the canal with Chabert from 10 p.m. to half past ten, with the torch. Chabert wanted to tell the gendarmes everything. Royer ran off when he saw a figure on the bridge. “When I left, he was alive.”
facts.label: Second interview

facts.text: Calls the miller “Aimé”. Swears “on the heads of my gones”, though he says he has no family left.
facts.label: The slip

clues.speaker: royer
clues.buttonAlone: Confront Lucien Royer with his lie

clues.title: Jacques Garcin
clues.text:
Royer looks at the identikit portrait, then at the 1992 photo Yves lays beside it. He takes off his cap. His hair is grey, cut short. He has the forehead from the photo, the nose, the chin. All he lacks is the moustache.

“My name is {{p:garcin|Jacques Garcin}}.”

He tells it without stopping, as if the words had been waiting for twenty months. The couple from Roanne who arrived late, on the evening of the 21st, pitch 31 at the back under the willows, “I told them we'd see about registering the next day”. The 22nd, the rain, the water rising, the evacuation with the list, everyone out, “everyone on the list”. And at six o'clock, in the middle of the car park, he remembered. “I ran. There was no back of the campsite any more. There were no willows any more. There was only the water.”

He pushed his car into the current at the ford. He climbed up into the hills. Aimé found him at two in the morning, sitting in the mud. “I said to him: say I'm dead. He said it. He made a hero of me, the idiot. He wanted to help me.”

The next evening he rang Hélène from a phone box in Malaucène. “I told her everything. She listened to the end. And then she said: You're dead. Stay dead. And she hung up.” The postal orders started arriving in November, poste restante at Buis. He cashed the first three, “in the winter, to eat”. Never again after that.

He puts his cap back on. “Do what you like with me. But I didn't kill Aimé. I loved him. He was the only one who knew.”

facts.text: Lucien Royer is Jacques Garcin. On 22 September 1992 he forgot the caravan on pitch 31, which was not registered. He pushed his car into the current and vanished. Chabert lied for him.
facts.label: His confession

facts.text: He rang her on 23 September 1992 from Malaucène. “You're dead. Stay dead.” She has known from the first day.
facts.label: According to Garcin

facts.text: He is Jacques Garcin. He cashed Hélène's first three postal orders, and none after that.
facts.label: His confession

clues.speaker: royer
clues.buttonAlone: Show Lucien Royer the identikit portrait

clues.title: Royer's hut
clues.text:
Royer's hut is at the far end of the orchard, a drystone shelter with a plank door and no lock. A camp bed, a basin, a camping stove, a 1993 Post Office calendar he has never changed.

On a shelf, an unframed photo held up by a drawing pin: two children on a pebble beach, a boy and a girl. Under the bed, a leather case. Inside, four bronze {{d:boules|lyonnaise boules}}, heavy as cobblestones, in felt compartments. On each one, engraved by hand, two initials: “J.G.”

In an iron sugar tin on the shelf, a bundle of {{d:mandats|postal orders}}, never cashed. Nineteen of them. Sender: “H. Garcin, Nyons”. Under the elastic band, a folded note in a woman's hand, very upright: “For your silence. For mine.”

Yves photographs the photo of the children, then puts it back exactly where it was, with the same drawing pin, in the same hole.

facts.text: Four bronze lyonnaise boules under Royer's bed, engraved “J.G.”.
Nineteen postal orders never cashed, sender “H. Garcin, Nyons”. A note: “For your silence. For mine.”
facts.label: In the hut

facts.text: A photo of two children, a boy and a girl. Boules engraved J.G. Hélène Garcin's postal orders.
facts.label: His hut

clues.button: Keep watch at night at Camping des Saules
clues.title: Night at Les Saules
clues.text:
It is eleven at night. Karim and Yves are crouching behind the wall of the old shower block at Camping des Saules, which no longer has a roof. The moon lights up the concrete slabs of the pitches, the twisted pipes, the bed of pebbles where the Ouvèze barely flows, so low you could cross it in your socks. The cicadas have gone quiet. You can hear the crickets, and an owl.

At twenty past eleven, a moped with no headlight. It stops at the entrance. A man walks to the far end, under what is left of the willows. He sets a glass jar on the ground and lights a candle inside it. He crouches in front of it. He is two metres from Karim.

The flame lights his face from below.

clues.title: The campsite ruins
clues.text:
In daylight, Camping des Saules looks like a bombed town in miniature. The slabs of the numbered pitches, the roofless shower block, a rusty sign, “ACCUEIL · RECEPTION · EMPFANG”, hanging by a single bolt. The vegetation has taken over everywhere except on the slabs.

At the far end, near the river, where nothing is left but the stumps of torn-out willows, a cross made of two branches bound with wire. In front of it, a jar with the stub of a candle. Wild flowers, poppies and lavender, cut a day or two ago. On the cross, two first names carved carefully with a knife: “Thierry · Nathalie”.

Yves looks for the pitch number. The marker post has fallen into the grass. He stands it up: 31.

“The memorial plaques give the names,” says Paul. “They don't say where the caravan was. Whoever comes here knows it to within a metre.”

facts.text: On pitch 31, at the back under the willows, a cross of branches carved “Thierry · Nathalie”, fresh flowers and a candle. Someone knows exactly where the caravan was.
facts.label: The ruins

clues.title: Rosa Bérenger
clues.text:
{{p:rosa|Rosa Bérenger}} is sitting on the bench facing the memorial, in the shade, a promotional fan in one hand and a rosary in the other. She is sixty-eight, with an Italian accent she hasn't lost in fifty years of the Vaucluse, and a photo of her husband in her handbag, which she takes out before anyone asks.

“Marius. Forty-one years married. The river took him in the cellar, he'd gone down to fetch the wine.” She puts the photo away. “Last Thursday I saw him at the market. In front of the cheese stall. He was wearing his jacket. He looked at me, and he went away.”

She doesn't cry. She explains, patiently, as if to children. “Since the photo in the paper, everyone knows. The river gives back its dead, monsieur. It kept Garcin two years, and it gave him back. It will give back the others.”

Paul doesn't contradict her. Karim writes everything down.

“And at night there's a light at {{l:camping_saules|Camping des Saules}}. A little light, at the back. I see it from my window, I live on the Malaucène road. It's them. They come back to where they left.”

facts.text: Widow of Marius, who died in the flood. Says she saw him at the market on Thursday 9 June. “The river gives back its dead. It gave back Garcin.”
At night, a little light shines at the back of the ruined campsite.
facts.label: According to Rosa

clues.speaker: rosa

clues.title: The memorial plaque
clues.text:
The memorial is a white stone stele on the bank of the Ouvèze, near the Roman bridge at Vaison, which held in 1992 when everything else was going. The names are carved in columns, in alphabetical order. There are always flowers.

Under G: “Jacques GARCIN, 1944-1992, died going to the rescue”. It is the only name with an inscription. In a porcelain medallion, the {{d:coupure_1992|photo}} from the 1992 newspaper: a moustached man with brown hair, a high forehead, a crooked nose, a square chin.

Under M: “Thierry MOLLET, 1966-1992”. Under B: “Nathalie BRUN, 1968-1992”.

Beneath Garcin's medallion, a bunch of lavender, fresh, held with an elastic band. A florist's card with no letterhead tucked into it, with a single word in biro: “Sorry.” No signature. Paul turns it over. Nothing on the back.

facts.text: On the Vaison plaque, the photo of Garcin in 1992: moustache, brown hair, high forehead, crooked nose, square chin.
facts.label: The medallion

facts.text: “Jacques GARCIN, died going to the rescue”, the only name with an inscription. Further down, Thierry Mollet and Nathalie Brun. A bunch of flowers with a card: “Sorry.”
facts.label: The plaque

confrontation.title: Karim's grid
confrontation.instructions: Only one of the four is lying, and everything that person says is false. The others are telling the truth. The grids are your rough work: only your answers to Paul's questions count.

declarations.texte: I spent the evening at the Café des Arcades. Ask anyone you like.
The canal? I didn't set foot there all evening.
I had my boules with me, like every evening. I never let them out of my sight.
If I went out, it was to fetch a boule I'd left on La Digue. Nothing else.
A torch? At my age, I know every stone in this country.
I was neither by the water nor on La Digue.
I wasn't looking for anything, and I wasn't waiting for anyone.
The lyonnaise boule, I'm the one who had it. I picked it up off the ground, it was lying about.
Madame Garcin didn't have the paper. She stopped her subscription after the photo, everyone knows that.

indices.texte: Around 10 p.m., a woman alone near La Digue boules ground.
The torch was found on the bank of the canal: whoever was holding it was at the canal.
His 10 p.m. customer at the Arcades watched the door all evening: the person at the Arcades was waiting for someone.
The miller was to “have it out with someone, at the canal, tonight”: the person at the canal had come to have it out.

questions.texte: Where was the liar at 10 p.m.?
What did Hélène Garcin have in her bag?

confrontation.erreur: “Granted.” Paul isn't convinced. Something doesn't hold up, and you have lost an hour.
confrontation.help: Karim taps two lines in his notepad. “Royer and Sandrine both say they had the lyonnaise boule. They can't both be telling the truth. The liar is one of those two.”
confrontation.result:
Paul nods. Lucien Royer lied about everything. At 10 p.m. he was on the bank of the canal, with the lamp from the Camping des Saules, come to have it out with the miller. Firmin was watching from the Roman bridge, his newspaper in his hand. Sandrine was looking for her watch at La Digue and had picked up Royer's boule there.

And Hélène Garcin was waiting at the Arcades, with {{d:cles_moulin|the mill keys}} in her bag. The keys she says she gave back in May.

“Granted, he's lying,” says Paul. “That doesn't mean he killed anyone. It means he was there.”

facts.text: Lies about everything. At 10 p.m. he was on the bank of the canal, with the lamp, come to have it out with the miller.
facts.label: The board

facts.text: In Hélène Garcin's bag, at the Arcades, on Wednesday at 10 p.m. She says she gave them back in May.
At the Arcades at 10 p.m., waiting for someone, with the mill keys in her bag.
facts.label: The board

facts.text: On the Roman bridge at 10 p.m., with that day's paper. He was watching someone.
facts.label: The board

facts.text: At La Digue at 10 p.m., with Royer's lyonnaise boule. She was looking for something she had lost.
facts.label: The board

portrait.title: The identikit portrait
portrait.instructions: Choose each feature from what the two witnesses say. When they disagree, ask yourself which of them could have got it wrong, and why.

temoins.texte: I watched him play all afternoon, from a distance, in full sun. And in the evening I gave him back his boule under the street lamp. Short hair, grey. A high forehead, with lines, three of them. A moustache, I think. Well. I've looked at that man in the paper so often. A square chin. I didn't look him in the eye.

I saw him from two metres away, by the light of the candle. White hair, pure white. Deep-set eyes, like two holes. A broken nose, crooked, like a boxer's. No moustache: clean-shaven, he had a razor nick on his cheek. A square chin, with a dimple.

portrait.wrongOne: Sandrine and Karim look at the portrait. They disagree with you on one feature.
portrait.wrongMany: Sandrine and Karim look at the portrait. They disagree with you on {n} features.
portrait.help: Yves picks up the overlays again. “Sandrine added the moustache from the 1992 paper: she looked at that photo every night for twenty months. And by candlelight, grey turns white. I know, it's my job.”
portrait.result:
Yves lays the {{d:portrait_robot|portrait}} next to the 1992 photo, the one in the medallion at Vaison. He covers the moustache with his thumb.

The same high forehead. The same deep-set eyes. The same broken nose, bent to the left. The same dimple in the chin. He takes his thumb away, puts it back.

“Twenty months, grey hair and a shave. It's him.”

facts.text: Short grey hair, high lined forehead, deep-set eyes, broken nose, thin mouth with no moustache, square dimpled chin. Garcin's face in 1992, without the moustache.
The man at La Digue and the man at the Saules are one and the same. He has Jacques Garcin's face, minus the moustache.
facts.label: The portrait

poursuite.title: Eight seconds
poursuite.instructions: He blows out the candle and gets to his feet. He is about to leave. Decide, fast.
poursuite.result: Karim saw him from two metres away, by the flame. Later he will turn it into his {{d:temoignage_karim|statement}} for Yves, word for word: “I saw him from two metres away, by the light of the candle. White hair, pure white. Deep-set eyes, like two holes. A broken nose, crooked, like a boxer's. No moustache: clean-shaven, he had a razor nick on his cheek. A square chin, with a dimple.”

options.text:
Karim doesn't move. Neither does Yves. The man stands there a long while in the dark, the dead candle at his feet. Then he speaks, very low, with an accent that isn't from round here.

“Sorry, Thierry. Sorry, Nathalie. I never put you down. I'd said tomorrow.”

He picks up the jar, walks back to the moped, and rides off without switching on the headlight.

options.text:
You let him go, then Yves starts the car with all its lights off. The moped doesn't go back up towards Les Pilles. It goes down towards Vaison, crosses the Roman bridge and stops in front of the {{l:memorial|memorial}}.

The man stands before the stone. Then he lays his hand flat on a name, under the letter G, and leaves it there a long time, as if on someone's shoulder.

When he has gone, Karim goes to look. Under his hand it said: Jacques GARCIN.

options.label: Block his way
options.text:
Yves stands up and fires his flash full in the man's face. The man cries out, hides his face in the crook of his arm and runs off through the stumps, towards the river. He leaves the moped behind, and a haversack at the foot of the cross.

Inside, a water bottle, a knife, and a {{d:photo_famille|photo}} folded in four, worn along the creases: a man with a moustache, a blonde woman, two children, in front of a sign reading “Camping des Saules”. On the back: “Summer 1991”.

In the morning, the moped has gone. Yves's photo, developed the next day: a raised arm, a white flare. Nothing else.

facts.text: In the haversack of the man from the Saules: the Garcin family in front of the campsite, “Summer 1991”.

options.label: Jump him
options.text:
Karim leaps. He played rugby at school, as he often tells people. The man is heavier, older, stronger. They roll over the pebbles. The cap falls off. The man pulls free, hits Karim just once, on the shoulder, without malice, and vanishes into the dark.

Two minutes later, headlights: a patrol from the Vaison gendarmerie, called out by a neighbour who can see “lights among the dead”. Karim spends the night in custody for assault. Yves spends it in the corridor, on a chair.

{{p:montagne|Warrant Officer Montagne}} comes to collect them at noon the next day. “Your trainee rugby-tackled a man on a ruined campsite. I don't have a column for that either. Full stop.” In the car, Karim takes the cap out of his pocket. He kept it. On the leather band, in ink: “J.G.”

You have lost a day.

endings.title: The front page
endings.headline: The drowned man of the Ouvèze was alive, and his widow knew
endings.text:
On Saturday 25 June, the Occult Affairs page is on the front of Le Drômois, and picked up by the group's thirteen other titles. Jean-Loup chose the headline himself: “The drowned man of the Ouvèze was alive, and his widow knew”.

Hélène Garcin is charged with murder the following Monday, in Valence. She says almost nothing to the judge. She asks only that her children not attend the trial. Dr Sauvan gives evidence. Warrant Officer Montagne is transferred to Die.

Jacques Garcin turns himself in at the Vaison gendarmerie on Tuesday morning, on foot, carrying a bag. The prosecutor's office in Carpentras reopens the flood file. He has no lawyer, and he doesn't want one.

Julien Garcin rings the Bureau in July. He doesn't shout. He only asks what his father looks like now. Paul tells him, feature by feature, as if for an identikit portrait.

endings.title: The motive
endings.headline: Nyons: hero's widow charged
endings.text:
On Saturday 25 June, the article causes a stir: the hero's widow killed the miller, and the hero is alive. Hélène Garcin is charged.

But the article gets the why wrong, and her lawyer knows it. At the September hearing he reads the Saturday page aloud, slowly, and asks the judge where the motive is. There isn't one, in what the Bureau wrote. Hélène Garcin is released under judicial supervision.

She takes the mill shop back in November, for the olive season. The customers say she is very dignified.

endings.title: The legend
endings.headline: Nyons: the miller did not drown on his own
endings.text:
On Saturday 25 June, the article holds up on one point: Aimé Chabert did not drown on his own. Hélène Garcin is questioned, then charged.

But the article doesn't say who the man in the photo is. The revenant remains a revenant. On Monday, Lucien Royer doesn't turn up at the orchards. Tardieu finds the hut empty, the boules bag gone, and the postal orders too.

In Vaison, the plaque still says “died going to the rescue”. Rosa Bérenger still sees Marius at the market. And at night, from her window, she no longer sees a light at the Camping des Saules.

endings.title: The revenant
endings.headline: The revenant of the Ouvèze killed the miller
endings.text:
On Saturday 25 June, Jean-Loup's headline goes round the whole region: “The revenant of the Ouvèze killed the miller”. It is exactly the page he wanted. Sales of Le Drômois double.

The gendarmes come for Lucien Royer at Les Pilles on Monday morning. He doesn't resist. He doesn't defend himself. He says only that his name is Jacques Garcin, and that he didn't kill Aimé. Nobody listens to him. They listen even less once they learn what he did in 1992.

Hélène Garcin sells the house in Les Forts in August, to a Dutch couple. Dr Sauvan sends the judge the results of her analysis, with a four-page letter. She never gets a reply.

endings.title: The denial
endings.headline: Nyons: the river keeps its secrets
endings.text:
The article comes out on Saturday 25 June. On Monday, the gendarmerie issues a statement: Aimé Chabert's death was accidental, the investigation is closed, and “certain journalists would do better to stick to ghosts”. Warrant Officer Montagne wrote the last sentence himself.

Jean-Loup summons Paul to Lyon. The door stays shut for an hour. When Paul comes out, he says only: “Granted.”

In Nyons, the mill's sluice gate is closed and the padlock is new. The summer goes by. They only press in winter.

Q4.right: The Vaison plaque is remade in October. The words “died going to the rescue” disappear, and Jacques Garcin's name with them. On the new stone, under the names of Thierry Mollet and Nathalie Brun, someone has had a line added: “pitch 31”.
Q4.wrong: In Vaison, the plaque still says “died going to the rescue”. Every 22 September, someone leaves a bunch of lavender there with a card: “Sorry.”

Q5.right: The Mutuelle rhodanienne files a complaint for fraud. The house in Les Forts is seized. Julien and Claire go to live with a great-aunt in Dieulefit.
Q5.wrong: The Mutuelle rhodanienne closes the file: nothing proves the widow knew. Jean-Claude Vasseur goes back to Avignon with his solar calculator.

Q6.right: Sandrine Mollet goes back to Roanne at the end of the month. Gaston Rey found Thierry's watch under a bench at La Digue. He took it to her at the campsite without a word, and left before she opened the box.
Q6.wrong: Sandrine Mollet is questioned three times by the gendarmes about her visit to the mill. She leaves Nyons before the apricots, without her watch.

frapper.title: The Bureau makes the front page
frapper.text: On Tuesday, La Gazette du Vaucluse, a rival paper, runs a headline on page 3: “Lyon journalist assaults farm worker at flood-hit campsite”. Jean-Loup cuts out the article and pins it above Karim's desk in Lyon. It stays there until Christmas.

cases.epilogue:
The following Monday, in the Bureau's post in Lyon, there is a plain white card with a Nyons postmark. The salamander in the flames, in red ink. On the back, in a fine, slanting hand: “Your conclusions are correct. So are ours. F. A.”

Odile puts it next to the one from November. The two salamanders are identical, down to the last stroke. That evening she stays late in the archives.

The next morning, on Paul's desk, there is a cutting from Le Drômois of 3 August 1958, from the boules page: “Nyons. Death of M. Firmin Achard, 71, a leading figure of la Boule nyonsaise.” No photo. Odile says nothing. She has underlined the age.
cases.solution: On 22 September 1992, Jacques Garcin evacuates his Camping des Saules with the list of guests, but he has forgotten to put on it the caravan of Thierry Mollet and Nathalie Brun, who arrived the day before. They die. Garcin disappears, and his friend Aimé Chabert, the miller, swears he saw him swept away while going to the rescue. The next day, Garcin rings his wife, Hélène: “You're dead. Stay dead.” She collects 1.4 million francs in life insurance and sends him postal orders to keep him quiet. Garcin lives at Les Pilles under the name Lucien Royer. In June 1994, a photo from a competition gives him away. Sandrine Mollet, Thierry's sister, recognises him, goes and shouts at Chabert's door and writes to the Bureau. Chabert decides to tell the gendarmes everything on Thursday 16, and warns Hélène. On Wednesday 15 at 10 p.m., he sees Garcin on the bank of the canal; Garcin leaves at half past ten, and Chabert is alive. At 11.05 p.m., Hélène enters the mill with her keys, puts Chabert to sleep with her Mogadon in a glass of marc, opens the sluice gate and pushes him into the millrace. Firmin Achard saw everything from the Roman bridge, and said nothing.

prologue.copie: Yves Barral, Karim Haddou, Odile Perrichon
corps: Our surveys are unanimous: the Saturday reader wants mystery. From 6 November, all fourteen of our dailies will carry a shared page every Saturday, “Occult Affairs”: haunted houses, faith healers, unexplained phenomena. The concept is simple, the readership is broad.

You will be in charge of it. You will have the old archive room on the fourth floor, Yves Barral for the photographs, and Karim Haddou, an intern, who volunteered. Odile Perrichon, in the archives, remains at your disposal.
Each week you will go wherever our readers report something strange. The local newsroom will put you up. The page goes to press on Thursdays at 6 p.m. Expense claims will be examined one by one.
I am counting on you to give me ghosts, not politics. Are we agreed?
